paras: The name Jongno comes from Jongnu (the bell pavilion). In the Joseon era, a bell pavilion with a big bell stood where Jongno 1-ga is today. The bell told people when the city gates opened and closed. When Seoul started its district system in 1943, the area became Jongno-gu, meaning "the street with the bell pavilion."

Many cultural heritage sites from the Joseon era are here, such as Gyeongbokgung Palace, Changdeokgung Palace, Changgyeonggung Palace, Jongmyo Shrine (the royal ancestral shrine), and Sajikdan (the altar for the gods of land and grain). Near the Sejong-ro intersection stands the Doroweonpyo (Road Origin Marker). It is the starting point used for road signs across the country.

paras: Jung-gu is in the middle of Seoul, inside the Four Great Gates. To the north, it meets Jongno-gu along Cheonggyecheon (Cheonggye Stream). To the south is Namsan (Namsan Mountain).

In 1943, Seoul (then called Gyeongseong-bu) started its district system with seven offices. Jung-gu began as one of them, the Central Office, and became the Jung-gu Ward Office that same year. In 1946, it was raised to Jung-gu of Seoul. It is a business center where banks have their head offices and large companies gather. It is also a shopping center with department stores and big markets.

paras: The Yongsan-gu Office says that Yongsan-gu began in 1896 as Yongsanbang (Yongsan district) of Hanseong-bu (the old Seoul). The name Yongsan-gu was given in October 1945, after liberation.

A neighborhood in Yongsan-dong 2-ga, on the southern slope of Namsan (Namsan Mountain), is called Haebangchon ("Liberation Village"). After liberation in 1945, Koreans who came back from abroad and people who came down from the north settled on this slope.

paras: The name Seongdong means 'east of the city wall'. In the Joseon era, if you left the capital's city wall through Gwanghuimun Gate, a wide field spread out to the east. This field was also called 'Salgoji-deul' (Salgoji Fields).

Seongdong-gu is one of the seven gu (Jongno, Jung, Yongsan, Dongdaemun, Seodaemun, Seongdong, and Yeongdeungpo) that were created when Seoul first set up gu in 1943. At one time, it also covered today's Gangnam and Gwangjin areas. Gangnam-gu split off in 1975, and Gwangjin-gu split off on March 1, 1995. The area of Seongdong-gu is 16.799 km², which is 2.8% of Seoul.

paras: The name Gwangjin comes from 'Gwangnaru'. There was a wide ferry crossing near Gwangjingyo (Gwangjin Bridge) in today's Gwangjang-dong, so it is said to have also been called 'Neobeunnaru' (Wide Ferry).

This area joined Seoul in 1949 from Ttukdo-myeon, Goyang-gun, Gyeonggi-do, and it belonged to Seongdong-gu for a long time. On March 1, 1995, Seongdong-gu was divided in two along Jungnangcheon Stream and Dongil-ro, and Gwangjin-gu was created. The area of Gwangjin-gu is 17.08 km², which is 2.8% of Seoul.

paras: The name Dongdaemun-gu comes from its location outside Dongdaemun (Heunginjimun Gate), one of the four great gates of the capital's city wall.

When the gu system was introduced in Seoul in 1943, the Eastern Branch Office was divided into Dongdaemun-gu and Seongdong-gu. After that, Seongbuk-gu split off in 1949. On January 1, 1988, Myeonmok-dong, Sangbong-dong, Mangu-dong, and other areas split off to become Jungnang-gu. The area of Dongdaemun-gu is 14.25 km².

paras: The land of Jungnang-gu was originally part of Guri-myeon, Yangju-gun, and Ttukdo-myeon, Goyang-gun, in Gyeonggi-do. Myeonmok-ri joined Seoul in 1949, and the Sangbong, Junghwa, Muk, Mangu, and Sinnae areas joined in 1963.

On January 1, 1988, gu that had become too crowded were divided, and five new gu were created: Jungnang, Nowon, Seocho, Yangcheon, and Songpa. Jungnang-gu was split from Dongdaemun-gu at this time. Around Mangusan, Bonghwasan, and Yongmasan (three mountains), relics from the Paleolithic and Bronze Ages have been found.

paras: The name Seongbuk-gu simply means 'north of the city wall'. It has cultural heritage such as the Seoul City Wall (Hanyangdoseong), Jeongneung (a royal tomb), and the Gansong Art Museum.

Seongbuk-gu was created on August 13, 1949, by combining Donam-dong, Anam-dong, and Seongbuk-dong of Dongdaemun-gu with several villages of Sungin-myeon, Goyang-gun, Gyeonggi-do. The Mia-ri, Beon-ri, Suyu-ri, and Ui-ri areas that came in at that time belonged to Dobong-gu in 1973 and became Gangbuk-gu in 1995. The area of Seongbuk-gu is 24.57 km², which is 4.06% of Seoul.

paras: Gangbuk-gu has four legal dong: Mia-dong, Beon-dong, Suyu-dong, and Ui-dong. In the Joseon era, these four neighborhoods belonged to Sungsin-bang in the eastern district of Hanseong-bu (the capital city district).

This area joined Seoul on August 13, 1949, and belonged to Seongbuk-gu. From 1973, it belonged to the newly created Dobong-gu. Later, as the population of Dobong-gu grew, it was divided again, and on March 1, 1995, Gangbuk-gu was created from these four dong.

paras: The name Dobong-gu was taken from Dobongsan (Mt. Dobong), the mountain that stands for this area. Dobongsan is a mountain with tall granite rock peaks, and its highest peak is Jaunbong (Jaunbong Peak).

Dobong-gu was created on July 1, 1973, when it was split from Seongbuk-gu. After that, Nowon-gu split off from Dobong-gu on January 1, 1988, and Gangbuk-gu split off on March 1, 1995. The area of Dobong-gu is 20.84 km², which is 3.44% of Seoul, and parks such as Bukhansan National Park cover more than half of the gu.

paras: In the Joseon era, this area had Nowon-myeon and Haedeungchon-myeon of Yangju. The Nowon-gu Office explains that these two were combined to become today's Nowon. Near Sanggye Elementary School, there is a place called 'Wonteo' because it was the site of the old Nowon-yeok (a relay station) and Nowon-won (an inn).
Nowon-gu was created on January 1, 1988, when it was split from Dobong-gu. At that time, Jungnang-gu, Seocho-gu, Yangcheon-gu, and Songpa-gu were also newly created.

paras: The name Eunpyeong comes from two names. They are Yeoneunbang and Sangpyeongbang, villages outside the city wall in the northern part of Hanseong-bu (the old Seoul) in the Joseon era.

This area was Eunpyeong-myeon in Goyang-gun, Gyeonggi-do, until it joined Seodaemun-gu in Seoul in 1949. In 1973, the Gupabal and Jingwan areas of Goyang-gun also became part of Seoul. On October 1, 1979, Eunpyeong-gu was split off from Seodaemun-gu.

paras: The name Seodaemun ("West Great Gate") comes from Donuimun (Donuimun Gate), the western gate of the four great gates of the city wall in the Joseon era. This gate was also called Seodaemun. The area below that gate got the regional name Seodaemun.

The Seodaemun Ward Office opened in 1943, and it became the Seodaemun-gu Office in October 1945. In 1949, parts of Eunpyeong-myeon and Yeonhui-myeon in Goyang-gun, Gyeonggi-do, joined Seodaemun-gu. In 1979, the northern neighborhoods such as Nokbeon-dong and Bulgwang-dong were split off to become Eunpyeong-gu. The name Hongeun-dong was made from "Hong" in the old Hongjeoe-ri and "Eun" in Eunpyeong-myeon.

paras: Mapo-gu was created on October 23, 1944, from parts of Seodaemun-gu and Yongsan-gu.
Its area is 23.85 km², about 3.9% of Seoul. Among its neighborhoods, Sangam-dong is the largest at 8.40 km². It is more than one third of the area of Mapo-gu.

paras: The name Yangcheon has been used since 1310, in the Goryeo era. The Yangcheon-gu Office describes Yangcheon as "a beautiful place where the bright sun shines and a stream flows." In the Joseon era, it was used as the name of a county, Yangcheon-hyeon.

The land of today's Yangcheon-gu moved from Gimpo-gun, Gyeonggi-do, to Yeongdeungpo-gu in Seoul in 1963. It belonged to Gangseo-gu in 1977, and on January 1, 1988, it was split off from Gangseo-gu to become Yangcheon-gu. Its area is about 17.4 km².

paras: Most of today's Gangseo-gu was once villages in Yangdong-myeon and Yangseo-myeon of Gimpo-gun, Gyeonggi-do. In 1963, the area joined Yeongdeungpo-gu in Seoul. On September 1, 1977, Gangseo-gu was created from 16 neighborhoods of Yeongdeungpo-gu.
On January 1, 1988, Mok-dong, Sinjeong-dong, and Sinwol-dong were split off to become Yangcheon-gu. The area is 41.46 km². More than half of it, 54.3%, is green zones (as of January 1, 2026).

paras: The name Guro comes from a legend that nine old men once lived here for a long time. In Chinese characters, it is written with 'gu' (九, nine) and 'ro' (老, old).

Guro-gu was created on April 1, 1980, when the southern part of Yeongdeungpo-gu was split off. At first, areas such as Doksan-dong and Siheung-dong, which are now in Geumcheon-gu, were also part of Guro-gu. They were separated when Geumcheon-gu was created on March 1, 1995.

paras: The name Geumcheon comes from Geumcheon-hyeon (an old county), which was created in 1413, during the reign of King Taejong of Joseon. The name was used for more than 380 years, until it was changed to Siheung-hyeon in 1795.

Geumcheon-gu was newly created on March 1, 1995, from Doksan-dong and Siheung-dong of Guro-gu and part of Garibong-dong (now Gasan-dong). So Geumcheon-gu has only three legal dong: Gasan-dong, Doksan-dong, and Siheung-dong.

paras: It is not certain where the name Yeongdeungpo came from. The Yeongdeungpo-gu Office says that many explanations see it as 'yeongdeung', which is linked to yeongdeung-gut (a traditional shaman ritual), plus 'po' (浦), which means waterside.

Yeongdeungpo-gu is one of the first seven gu created in Seoul in 1943. Today its area is 24.35 km² (4.02% of Seoul). But Gwanak-gu in 1973, Gangseo-gu in 1977, and Guro-gu in 1980 were all created from land that belonged to Yeongdeungpo-gu.

paras: The name Dongjak comes from Dongjaegi-naru (Dongjaegi Ferry), an old ferry crossing on the Hangang (Han River). In the Joseon era, this crossing was on the road linking the southern regions with Seoul, so many people and goods passed through.
Dongjak-gu was split off from Gwanak-gu on April 1, 1980, and became the 17th gu of Seoul. Its area is 16.39 km², which is 2.7% of Seoul.

paras: The name 'Gwanak' was first used as an administrative name in 1963. That year, a 'Gwanak Branch Office' was set up to manage the land of Dong-myeon, Siheung-gun, Gyeonggi-do, which had newly joined Seoul. On July 1, 1973, the area was split from Yeongdeungpo-gu and became Gwanak-gu.

At first, Gwanak-gu also included the land of today's Dongjak-gu and parts of Seocho-gu, such as Bangbae-dong, Seocho-dong, and Banpo-dong. On April 1, 1980, Noryangjin-dong, Sangdo-dong, and other areas were split off to become Dongjak-gu. The area of Gwanak-gu is 29.56 km², which is 4.9% of Seoul.

paras: The name Seocho comes from an old name, Seoripul. The Seocho-gu Office explains that "seocho" means a plant that brings good things to mind, that is, rice. It says there is a record that rice grown in Seocho-dong long ago was given to the king.

Seocho-gu was created on January 1, 1988. Eleven legal neighborhoods, including Seocho-dong, Banpo-dong, Bangbae-dong, and Yangjae-dong, were split off from Gangnam-gu. To the north, it faces Yongsan-gu across the Hangang (Han River). To the south, it meets Gwacheon and Seongnam in Gyeonggi-do.

paras: Gangnam-gu was created in 1975, when the Yeongdong Branch Office of Seongdong-gu was closed. At that time, Gangnam-gu was a large gu that covered today's Seocho-gu, Gangnam-gu, Songpa-gu, and Gangdong-gu together. Later, Gangdong-gu was split off in 1979, and Seocho-gu in 1988.

To the east, it meets Songpa-gu with Tancheon (Tan Stream) in between. To the west, it meets Seocho-gu along Gangnam-daero (Gangnam Boulevard). Its area is 39.5 km², which is 6.53% of Seoul. The largest neighborhood is Segok-dong.

paras: A few stories are told about where the name Songpa came from. One says that pine trees grew thickly on a hill in a village by the Hangang (Han River) long ago, so it was called "Pine Hill" (松坡).

This area belonged to Gangdong-gu, which was created in 1979. On January 1, 1988, Songpa-gu was split off from Gangdong-gu. In the Joseon era, Samjeondo (Samjeondo Ferry) on the Hangang here was counted as one of the three ferries of the Seoul section of the Hangang, along with Hangang-naru and Nodeul-naru.

paras: Gangdong-gu was created on October 1, 1979, when the Cheonho Branch Office became a gu. At first, it also included today's Songpa-gu. Songpa-gu was split off on January 1, 1988.

The Amsa-dong site by the Hangang (Han River) is the remains of homes where people lived in the Neolithic Age, about 6,000 to 5,000 years ago. It is one of the village sites in North and South Korea where the most house remains have been found. The remains are of umjip (pit houses), where people dug into the ground and covered the top with a roof.

paras: There are two stories about where the name Mokpo came from. One says it was a port south of Naju, so it was called Nampo and Malgpo before it became Mokpo. The other says the place played an important role like a neck (mok in Korean), so people called it 'Mokgae', and this was later written in Chinese characters. Mokpo City Hall describes the second story as the more likely one.

In the Joseon era, Mokpo had a naval camp. During the Imjin War (the Japanese invasions, 1592-1598), it kept legends of Admiral Yi Sun-sin and traces of the naval camp. The port was opened on October 1, 1897, and in 1910 the name changed to Mokpo-bu (Mokpo Prefecture). In 1949, after liberation, Mokpo-bu became Mokpo-si. In 1952, the first local election was held, a city council was formed, and a mayor was chosen.

sources.t: Mokpo City Hall, About Mokpo · History / Origin of the name

paras: In the 16th year of King Seong of Baekje (538), the Yeosu area was Wonchon-hyeon and Dolsan-hyeon (hyeon means county). In 757 the names changed to Haeeup-hyeon and Yeosan-hyeon, and in 940 to Yeosu-hyeon and Dolsan-hyeon. In 1949, Yeosu-eup (Yeosu town) was raised to Yeosu-si, and the other nine myeon (townships) became Yeocheon-gun. On April 1, 1998, Yeosu-si, Yeocheon-si, and Yeocheon-gun were joined to make today's Yeosu-si.

The Yeosu City Hall website describes Yeosu as the clear blue sea where the Hallyeosudo (Hallyeo Waterway) begins. In the 10th year of King Seongjong of Joseon (1479), the Jeollajwado Sugun Jeoldosa-yeong (the naval commander's headquarters of the Left Jeolla Province) was set up. In the 26th year of King Seonjo (1593), the Samdo Sugun Tongjeyeong (the Naval Command of the Three Provinces) was set up. In 2012, the Yeosu World Expo was held.

paras: In the 16th year of King Gyeongdeok of Unified Silla (757), Suncheon was called Seungpyeong-gun. In 1309, the first year of King Chungseon of Goryeo, it became Seungju-mok, and the next year it was lowered to Suncheon-bu. In 1413, the 13th year of Taejong of Joseon, Suncheon Dohobu (protectorate) was set up. In 1949 it was raised to Suncheon-si and the rest of the area became Seungju-gun. On January 1, 1995, Suncheon-si and Seungju-gun joined to become the new Suncheon-si.

The Suncheon City Hall website describes the map of Suncheon as looking like the head of a cow. Unryong-ri in Juam-myeon and Bichon-ri in Hwangjeon-myeon are the cow's two horns, and parts of Haeryong-myeon and Byeollyang-myeon are the mouth. Seungju-eup is said to be near the top of the head, in the very center of the city. Suncheon borders Gwangyang-si, Gurye-gun, Gokseong-gun, Hwasun-gun, Boseong-gun, and Yeosu-si, and part of its south touches the sea of Suncheon Bay and Gwangyang Bay.

paras: In the Samhan period, Naju belonged to the 54 small states of Mahan. In the Baekje period it was called Balla and Tongui. In Unified Silla it was Geumseong-gun (Geumsan), and in 903 it received the name Naju. In 983, in the Goryeo period, Naju-mok was set up as one of the 12 mok (large provincial districts) in the country. In 1018 it became one of the 8 mok in the country.

In 1011, the Khitan invaded, and Naju briefly became a capital, where the king stayed after fleeing from the invasion. Naju-mok continued until 1895. That year a Naju county governor was appointed and Naju Gwanchalbu (the Naju provincial office) was set up. In 1981, Naju-eup and Yeongsanpo-eup became Geumseong-si, and in 1986 the name was changed to Naju-si. In 1995, Naju-si and Naju-gun were joined.

sources.t: Naju City Hall, About Naju · Status of Naju · History

paras: Gwangyang was called Maro in the Baekje period and Huiyang in the Unified Silla period. From the Goryeo period it was called Gwangyang. Gwangyang City Hall explains that 'Maro' means chief, and that 'Huiyang' and 'Gwangyang' mean warmly shining sunlight. In 940, under King Taejo of Goryeo, Huiyang-hyeon was renamed Gwangyang-hyeon. In 1172 it was split off from Seungpyeong-gun and came to be governed by an official called a gammu.

In 1989, the Gwangyang District Branch Office of Jeollanam-do became Donggwangyang-si. In 1995, Donggwangyang-si and Gwangyang-gun joined to become Gwangyang-si, a city with both urban and rural areas. Stone tools from the Paleolithic period were found here, so people are thought to have lived here since the Paleolithic period. Dolmens (Bronze Age tombs) have also been surveyed in several places.

paras: Dong-gu opened on July 1, 1973, when the gu (district) system began. It was made by joining the Jungbu, Dongbu, and Bukbu branch offices, and its first office building was in Geumnam-ro 2-ga. On May 1, 1988, it became a self-governing gu.

Dongmyeong-dong was outside the east gate of the old Gwangju Eupseong (town fortress), so it was called 'Dongbakae', and in 1946 it received the name Dongmyeong-dong. Gyerim-dong is said to have become Gyerim-dong in 1947 because trees grew thickly on the bank of Gyeongyang Bangjuk (Gyeongyang Pond) and residents raised many chickens, so the crowing of chickens could be heard. Hak-dong became Hak-dong in 1947 because the ridge of Mudeungsan (Mt. Mudeung) comes down like a crane (hak) and settles on the hill. Sansu-dong was called Sansu because it is a neighborhood with beautiful mountains and water.

paras: Seo-gu opened on July 1, 1973, when the gu (district) system began, by joining the Nambu, Seobu, and Jisan branch offices. At that time it had 45 dong (neighborhoods). On April 1, 1980, Buk-gu was split off. On May 1, 1988, it became a self-governing gu, and on March 1, 1995, Nam-gu was split off.

On April 20, 1995, it took in Seochang-dong from Gwangsan-gu. On October 1, 2011, it took in parts of Dongnim-dong and Unam-dong from Buk-gu, and Dongcheon-dong was newly created. The mountains Geumdangsan, Gaegeumsan, and Songhaksan surround it like a folding screen. Seo-gu describes the Sangmu, Pungam, and Geumho districts as proud of their pleasant living environments. It has a terminal, so it is also a center of transportation.

paras: Nam-gu opened as a new gu on March 1, 1995, by splitting off from Seo-gu. At first it had 18 dong (neighborhoods), including Yangnim-dong. Then Bongseon-dong was split in two, making 19 dong. On April 20 of the same year, it took in the Daechon branch office of Gwangsan-gu, and this became Daechon-dong.

The Nam-gu area was handled by the Nambu branch office in 1961. On July 1, 1973, when the gu system began, it became part of Seo-gu, which was formed by joining the Nambu, Seobu, and Jisan branch offices. In Daechon-dong, the Geungnakgang River and the Jiseokcheon Stream flow to the west and south, and fertile fields spread along the Daechoncheon Stream. The area centers on horticulture (garden-crop farming). Nam-gu describes cultural heritage there such as Gossaum Nori (a traditional folk game), Pochungsa Shrine, and Jisanjae.

paras: On July 1, 1973, when the gu (district) system began, the Buk-gu area was split between Dong-gu and Seo-gu. The Seokgok branch office and the Jisan branch office handled 24 dong (neighborhoods). By a presidential decree announced in 1979, 19 dong such as Jungheung-dong, Usan-dong, Punghyang-dong, and Munhwa-dong, which had been handled by Dong-gu, Seo-gu, the Seokgok branch office, and the Jisan branch office, were gathered to set up Buk-gu.

Buk-gu describes itself as a center of transportation, with Gwangju Station and the Honam Expressway. It says it is a city of righteousness and of the arts, with the National 5·18 Democratic Cemetery and the Mudeungsan Siga Munhwagwon (the Mudeungsan poetry and verse cultural area). It also has several schools, such as Chonnam National University, the University of Education, and the Institute of Science and Technology. It is also a city of future high-tech industry, based on the Cutting-edge Industrial Complex and the Gwangju R&D Special Zone.

paras: Gwangsan-gu borders Hampyeong-gun to the west, Naju-si and Nam-gu to the south, and Jangseong-gun to the north. To the east are Seo-gu and Buk-gu. In 1895 it was Gwangju-gun. In 1935, when Gwangju-bu was set up as a separate unit, it became Gwangsan-gun, and in 1949 the county office moved to Songjeong-eup. In 1986, Songjeong-eup became Songjeong-si. In 1988, Songjeong-si and Gwangsan-gun were joined to make the new Gwangsan-gu.

In the east, the Geungnakgang River flows between fertile fields. In the south, the wide plains along the Hwangnyonggang River and the Geungnakgang River continue into the Naju Plain. In the north, the Sobaek Mountains and the Noryeong Mountains stretch out, so there are many mountains and hills. Gwangsan-gu describes itself as an important place for transportation, with well-developed air, rail, expressway, and national road links.

sources.t: Gwangsan-gu Office, About Gwangsan-gu · History

paras: The name Damyang was first used in the Goryeo period. In the Baekje period the area was called Chujahye-gun, and in the Silla period Chuseong-gun. In 995, under King Seongjong of Goryeo, the post of dodallyeonsa was set up in Damju. It is said that the name was later changed to the present one and the area was placed under Naju.

In 1395, under King Taejo of Joseon, it was raised to a gun (county). Later it was raised to a bu because it was the maternal family home of Queen Kim, and in 1413, under Taejong, it became a dohobu (protectorate). In 1914, Damyang-gun and Changpyeong-gun were joined to make today's Damyang-gun. In a 2001 survey, chipped stone tools from the Paleolithic period were found. Dolmens (Bronze Age tombs) are found in Daejeon-myeon, Mujeong-myeon, and other places.

sources.t: Damyang County Office, About Damyang · History of Damyang · History / Timeline

paras: In 475, under King Munju of Baekje, Gokseong was called Yongnae. In 757, under King Gyeongdeok of Unified Silla, the name changed to Gokseong-gun. In 1018, in the Goryeo period, it was placed under Naju-mok. In 1389, at the end of Goryeo, the town was destroyed by attacks from Japanese pirates. The center of the county moved from Dang-dong, Jukgok-myeon, to its present place below Dongaksan (Mt. Dongak).

In 1899 a county governor was appointed under the name Gokseong-gun. In 1914, land from parts of Damyang, Gurye, Suncheon, and Namwon came in, and the myeon (townships) were newly arranged. In 1979, Gokseong-myeon was raised to Gokseong-eup. The temple Taeansa (Taeansa Temple) was built in 742 and became the central temple of the Dongnisan school of Seon (Zen) Buddhism. The Sunjagang River, the main stream of the Seomjingang River, and the Boseonggang River join at Amnok and flow east.

paras: In the Samhan period, Gurye belonged to Gorap-guk (the state of Gorap). In the Baekje period it was called Gucharye-hyeon. In 1413, under Taejong of Joseon, it was raised to a hyeon (county). In 1499, under Yeonsangun, it was lowered from a hyeon to a bugok (a small local district) and belonged to Namwon-bu. In 1507 it became a hyeon again, and in 1895 it became Gurye-gun.

In 1906, four myeon (townships) of Namwon-gun in Jeollabuk-do came into Gurye: Sandong, Jungbang, Soui, and Godal. In 1914, Godal-myeon moved to Gokseong-gun, and the rest became eight myeon: Gurye, Ganmun, Toji, Masan, Gwangui, Yongbang, Oesan, and Naesan. In 1946, Ganmun-myeon was split into Munchok-myeon and Ganjeon-myeon. In 1963, Gurye-myeon was raised to Gurye-eup.

paras: The name Goheung is said to join 'Goi' from Goi Bugok (a small local district under Jangheung-bu in the Goryeo period) and 'heung' from Jangheung. In 1285 it was raised to Goheung-hyeon, and in 1441, under King Sejong of Joseon, the name changed to Heungyang-hyeon. In 1895 it became Heungyang-gun, and in 1914 the name was changed to Goheung-gun.

In the Joseon period, this area had the naval posts of Sado, Balpo, Nokdo, and Yeodo, which belonged to the Jeollajwasuyeong (the Left Jeolla Naval Command). During the Imjin War (the Japanese invasions, 1592-1598), they are said to have formed the main force of the fleet of Admiral Chungmu (Yi Sun-sin), and many local commanders are said to have done great deeds in the sea battles. A record from the time of King Yeongjo says that Goheung is a place with clear and beautiful mountains and sea. In 1973, Doyang-myeon was raised to Doyang-eup, and in 1979, Goheung-myeon was raised to Goheung-eup.

paras: In the Three Kingdoms period, Boseong was Mahan land. It was merged into Baekje (an ancient kingdom) in the time of King Geunchogo, and the county was then called "Bokhol." In the 16th year of King Gyeongdeok of Unified Silla (757), all county and prefecture names were changed to Chinese-style names, and the place was first called "Boseong-gun." In the 14th year of King Seongjong of Goryeo (995), it was renamed "Paeju." In the 9th year of King Hyeonjong (1018), it became Boseong-gun again.

Work on the Juam Multipurpose Dam (Juam Dagimokjeok Dam) began in 1984 and ended in 1991. Because of this dam, parts of some villages in Mundeok-myeon, Boknae-myeon, and Yureo-myeon went under water. The Boseong-gun website names three kinds of scenery in Boseong: mountains, a lake, and the sea. The mountains are Jeamsan, Jonjesan, and Jeseoksan. The lake is the Boseong River (Boseonggang), which flows into the Seomjin River (Seomjingang). In the sea, people raise shellfish such as cockles.

paras: In 940, in the Goryeo period, Yeomi-hyeon (a county-level district) was renamed Hwasun-hyeon, which is close to today's name. In the Baekje period, there were three hyeon in the Neungju, Hwasun, and Dongbok area. In the Joseon period, they continued as three towns: Neungju-mok, Hwasun-hyeon, and Dongbok-hyeon. In 1913, Neungju-gun was renamed Hwasun-gun. In 1914, Dongbok-gun was added too, and the county took its present form.

Hwasun-hyeon was once abolished because of the damage from a big war, but it was set up again in 1611. A ginkgo tree planted to mark this stands today at the Hwasun County Office. Hwasun has dolmens (ancient stone tombs) that are a World Heritage site. It also has traditional temples such as Unjusa Temple and Ssangbongsa Temple, and the Hwasun hot spring. It has rest areas too, such as the Mudeungsan Hinoki Cypress Natural Recreation Forest and the Manyeonsan Healing Forest Center.

paras: In the Goryeo period, Jeongan-hyeon (a county-level district) was raised to Jangheung-bu (prefecture), because it was the hometown of Queen Gongye, the queen of King Injong. In 1413, in the Joseon period, it became Jangheung Dohobu (protectorate). In 1895, it became Jangheung-gun of Naju-bu. The next year, 1896, it became Jangheung-gun of South Jeolla Province.

There are also signs that people lived here very long ago. At the Sinbuk site, more than 30,000 items were found, including leaf-shaped stone points from the Paleolithic period. More than 2,200 dolmens (ancient stone tombs) from the Bronze Age are spread across the upper Boseong River area, the Tamjin River area, and the south coast. In 1894, the Donghak peasant army lost at Seokdaeul in Jangheung. This was the place of the last big battle of the Donghak Peasant Revolution.

paras: The name Gangjin came from the joining of two areas, Dogang and Tamjin, in the Baekje period. The character "gang" (康) from Dogang and the character "jin" (津) from Tamjin were put together to make Gangjin (康津). In 1172, in the time of King Myeongjong of Goryeo, an official was sent here to handle both government and military matters. In 1895, when the local system was changed, it became Gangjin-gun.

In 1417, in the time of King Taejong of Joseon, the Jeolla Provincial Army Base (Jeolla-do Byeongyeong) was newly set up in what is now the Byeongyeong-myeon area. At that time, this place was named Gangjin-hyeon. In 1936, Gangjin-myeon was raised to Gangjin-eup. In 1989, the Maryang branch office became Maryang-myeon. In 1990, the Bonghwang-ri area of Okcheon-myeon in Haenam-gun was added to Doam-myeon.

paras: Haenam-gun is a place where three hyeon (county-level districts), including Saegeum-hyeon, were set up in 538, in the Baekje period. In the Unified Silla period, Saegeum-hyeon was renamed Chimmyeong-hyeon. In 940, in the Goryeo period, Chimmyeong-hyeon became Haenam-hyeon. In the Joseon period, it was merged with Jindo in 1409, then split again in 1437 and called Haenam-hyeon once more. In 1895 it became Haenam-gun of Naju-bu, and the next year it became Haenam-gun of South Jeolla Province.

Haenam is on the Haenam Peninsula. Only the east and northeast are land, connected to Gangjin and Yeongam, and the other three sides are sea. It borders Gangjin-gun to the east, Jindo-gun to the west, Wando-gun to the south, and Yeongam-gun to the north. The county office describes Haenam as the place at the very southern end of the Korean Peninsula, known as Ttangkkeut ("the end of the land").

paras: In the Baekje period, Yeongam was Wolla-gun. In 757, King Gyeongdeok of Unified Silla changed the name to Yeongam-gun. In the 14th year of King Seongjong of Goryeo (995), it was raised to Nangju, and a government office called Annam Dohobu was placed there. In the 9th year of King Hyeonjong (1018), that office was moved to Jeonju, and the place became Yeongam-gun again.

According to the Yeongam County website, Dr. Wang In (a scholar from Baekje) crossed to Japan in 405 after being invited by Japan. Sangdaepo in Yeongam is known as the port from which Wang In left for Japan. It is said that people such as Choe Chi-won also used Sangdaepo when they went to Tang China at the end of the Silla period. The website describes the Seated Buddha Carved in the Rock (Maae Yeorae Jwasang, National Treasure No. 144) on Wolchulsan Mountain as the largest rock-carved Buddha in Korea.

paras: In the 16th year of King Gyeongdeok of Unified Silla (757), Muan was Muan-gun of Muju. In the 2nd year of King Myeongjong of Goryeo (1172), it became Muan-hyeon. In the 13th year of King Taejong of Joseon (1413), it became Muan-hyeon of Jeolla Province, and a hyeongam (a county magistrate) was posted there. On January 1, 1969, Sinan-gun was split off from Muan-gun, and Muan-gun was left with the eight myeon on the mainland.

The Muan County website says that Muan is at the southwestern end of Korea and is surrounded by sea on three sides. To the east, across the Yeongsan River (Yeongsangang), it neighbors Naju City and Yeongam-gun. The land has many low mountains. The soil has a lot of sand and clay, and it is said to be good for growing onions, garlic, sweet potatoes, and sesame.

paras: The name Hampyeong came about in 1409, in the Joseon period, when Hampung-hyeon and Mopyeong-hyeon were merged. The character "ham" (咸) was taken from Hampung, and the character "pyeong" (平) was taken from Mopyeong. In 1413, a hyeongam (a county magistrate) was posted here. It became Hampyeong-gun in 1895, and in 1896 it became a county of South Jeolla Province.

It is thought that there were one or two small states in Hampyeong in the Mahan period. Dolmens (ancient stone tombs) from the Bronze Age were spread all over the county. In the Manga-chon tomb in Yedeok-ri, Woryeol-myeon, various items such as jars from the 2nd to 3rd centuries were found. In a stone-lined tomb in Chopo-ri, Nasan-myeon, Bronze Age items from the 2nd to 3rd centuries BC were found. They show that people who could make bronze lived here.

paras: The Yeonggwang County website says that the name Yeonggwang means "town of sacred light." In the Baekje period, it was Musii-gun. In the 16th year of King Gyeongdeok of Unified Silla (757), the name was changed to Muryeong-gun. In the 23rd year of King Taejo of Goryeo, Muryeong-gun became Yeonggwang-gun. From the 14th year of King Seongjong (995), it was called Jeongju, and in the 9th year of King Hyeonjong (1018), it went back to Yeonggwang.

It is said that in the time of King Chimnyu of Baekje, Maranta (Marananta), a high monk from India, came to what is now Jinnae-ri in Beopseong. This place is said to be where Buddhism first came to Baekje. In the 11th year of King Seongjong of Goryeo (992), a tax-grain storehouse called Buyongchang was opened at Buyongpo. In the time of King Munjong, its name was changed to Beopseongchang. In 1985, Hongnong-myeon was raised to Hongnong-eup, and the county has had 3 eup and 8 myeon since then.

paras: In the Unified Silla period, Jangseong-gun was Gapseong-gun. In 940, in the early Goryeo period, the name was changed to Jangseong-gun. In 1256, in the Goryeo period, Mongol troops were beaten back at Ibamsanseong Fortress. In 1894, the Donghak army won a big victory over the government army in the Battle of Hwangnyong. In 1896, it became Jangseong-gun of South Jeolla Province. In 1975, Buksang-myeon disappeared when Jangseong Lake was made.

Jangseong is described as a land of learning where the spirit of the seonbi (Confucian scholars) is alive. The saying "Munbulyeo Jangseong" ("no place is better than Jangseong for learning") is said to have come from a story that Heungseon Daewongun said, "For learning, there is no place like Jangseong." Pilamseowon (Pilam Confucian Academy) in Pilam-ri, Hwangnyong-myeon honors Kim In-hu. There are also other academies in many places, such as Gosanseowon and Bongamseowon.

paras: Wando-gun is at the southernmost part of the Korean Peninsula, and it is made up of many islands, big and small. In the old days it belonged to Saegeum-hyeon, which was Baekje land. In 828, in the Unified Silla period, Jang Bogo set up Cheonghaejin (the Cheonghae Garrison). In 1896, the islands that had belonged to Yeongam, Haenam, Gangjin, and Jangheung were put together to make Wando-gun.

In 1598, in the Joseon period, Admiral Yi Sun-sin set up the Samdo Sugun Tongjeyeong (the Three-Province Naval Command) on Gogeumdo Island. In 1637, Yun Seon-do settled on Bogildo Island. In the 1920s, an anti-Japanese movement rose on Soando Island. In 1969, Wando Bridge was built to link Haenam and Wando. In 2007, Cheongsando Island became the first Slow City in Asia.

paras: In the Baekje period, Jindo-gun was called Injindo-gun, and its government office was in what is now Goseong in Gogun-myeon. In 1409, in the Joseon period, it was merged with Haenam. In 1437, it was split again and became Jindo-gun. In 1440, the government office was moved to what is now Jindo-eup. In 1979, Jindo-myeon was raised to Jindo-eup.

The Jindo County Office describes Jindo as the place of the "Miracle Sea Road" (the sea parting) and Unrim Sanbang (Unrim Mountain House, a famous painter's home and garden). It also calls Jindo the home of Southern-style painting (Namhwa), calligraphy, and Namdo-chang (Namdo songs), and a site of battles that defended the nation. In 1270, in the Goryeo period, the Sambyeolcho (an elite military group) made Yongjangsa Temple their capital and fought against the Mongol army. Uldolmok Strait and Byeokpajin, where the Battle of Myeongnyang took place, are also in Jindo. The Jindo dog, goji berries (gugija), and wild seaweed (dolmiyeok) are said to be the "three treasures" (sambo).

paras: Sinan belonged to Mahan in very ancient times, and in the Japanese colonial period it belonged to Muan-gun. On January 1, 1969, it was split off from Muan-gun and became Sinan-gun. After that, Jido-myeon was raised to Jido-eup in December 1980, and Aphae-myeon was raised to Aphae-eup in the 2000s.

According to the Sinan County website, Dadohae Haesang National Park (Dadohae Marine National Park) was designated on December 23, 1981, as the 14th national park. It covers parts of Sinan-gun, Jindo-gun, Wando-gun, and Yeosu City. In Sinan-gun, Hongdo Island and parts of Heuksan-myeon, Bigeum-myeon, Docho-myeon, and Haui-myeon are inside this park. Sinan Tidal Flat Provincial Park (Sinan Gaetbeol Dorip Gongwon) was first designated in Jeungdo-myeon in 2008. In 2018, it was widened to cover all the other eup and myeon except Heuksan-myeon.

paras: In Jung-gu, Bosusan Mountain is the main mountain, and Busan Port (Busanhang) spreads out in front of it. The district is described as a small copy of all of Busan, with mountains at its back and the sea in front. Yongdusan Hill, which now seems to sit in the arms of Jung-gu, was once a low hill that stretched south from Bokbyeongsan Hill, at the foot of Bosusan.

When the port opened, merchants from all over the country gathered and settled in Yeongju-dong, and a new village grew. In 1889 a road opened, and a town took shape around Songhyeonsan (now Yongdusan). In 1910 Busan Station was built, and a railroad was laid to Pier No. 1. The pebbly shore of Nampo-dong was filled in with soil and became house lots and shopping areas.

paras: Seo-gu is in the southwest of Busan. Jung-gu and Dong-gu are to the east, Saha-gu is to the west, and Busanjin-gu and Sasang-gu are to the north. A branch office of Seo-gu was set up on September 1, 1951. When the city of Busan began its district system on January 1, 1957, Seo-gu was created. On January 1, 1963, Busan became a directly governed city (Jikhalsi), and the name of the office changed to 'Busan Jikhalsi Seo-gu Office'.

A mountain ridge runs from Gudeoksan, Eomgwangsan, and Siyaksan to Amisan, Cheonmasan, and Janggunsan, and the sea lies to the south. Songdo Beach is described as the first beach in Busan. There are also Amnam Park and Daesin Park. The Busan Joint Fish Market and the Busan International Fisheries Wholesale Market are here too, so it is a place where seafood gathers.

paras: Dong-gu is in the middle of Busan. It borders Jung-gu, Busanjin-gu, and Nam-gu, and it faces Busan North Port (Bukhang). When the city of Busan began its district system in 1957, Dong-gu was created. Choryang-dong, Sujeong-dong, Jwacheon-dong, and Beomil-dong are villages in Dong-gu.

Dong-gu is land that faces the sea with Sujeongsan and Gubongsan mountains behind it to the west. Most of it is sloped, so it was hard to build a flat town. During the Japanese colonial period, the shore was filled in, and about one third of the urban area was made this way. Most houses are on the high slopes of the two mountains. The district has grown along streams such as Choryangcheon, Busancheon, and Hogyecheon, and along mountain valleys.

paras: The old name of Yeongdo was Jeoryeongdo. The story says that a 'cheollima' (a legendary horse that runs a thousand ri a day) runs so fast that its shadow cannot keep up. So the island is said to have been named with the characters for 'cut off' (jeol, 絶) and 'shadow' (yeong, 影). After liberation, when administrative areas were reorganized, the old name Jeoryeongdo was shortened to the present name, Yeongdo.

From the Silla period to the middle of the Joseon period, Yeongdo was an island where horses were let loose to graze. It had a state horse ranch (gukmajang), and it is said that there were many fine horses. Dongsam-dong Shell Mound and Yeongseon-dong Shell Mound are here, so it is thought to be the first place in Busan where people lived. In 1881 a military camp called Jeoryeongdojin was built, and the number of residents slowly grew.

paras: The name Busanjin-gu comes from Busanjinseong Fortress (Busanjin Fortress), which stood on the road into Busan Port during the Imjin War (the Japanese invasions, 1592-1598). A branch office called Busanjin was set up in 1936. When the district system began in 1957, it became Busanjin-gu. In the Samhan period, it was land of the state of Geochilsan. In the Silla period, it was Dongpyeong-hyeon (a small district) in Dongnae County, and in the Joseon period, it belonged to Dongnae-bu (Dongnae Prefecture).

Bujeon-dong in Busanjin-gu once belonged to Buhyeon-ri in Dongnae-bu. It is said that the name Buhyeon seems to come from Gamagogae (Cauldron Pass), a pass with a rock shaped like an upside-down cauldron. Yeonji-dong had a pond, and it is said to have been where Yeonji Elementary School stands now.

paras: Dongnae-gu got the name Dongnae in 757, during the reign of King Gyeongdeok of Silla, when this land became Dongnae County. Dongnae means 'inner mountain of the east'. It is explained as a short form of Bongnaesan (Mount Bongnae), the mountain where immortals are said to live. When the district system began in 1957, it became Dongnae-gu.

The center of old Dongnae County was near Suyeong. In the Goryeo period, Japanese pirates often attacked, so the fortress was moved to where Dongnae-eup is now. In 1547, in the Joseon period, it was raised to a dohobu (protectorate). Cultural heritage and places here include the Dongnaeeupseong Fortress site (Dongnae Town Fortress), the Bokcheon-dong Tombs, Dongnae Hot Spring, and Geumgang Park. Dongnae-gu Office describes this land as a place of tradition and loyalty where the spirit of defending the nation has continued.

paras: Until it joined the city of Busan in 1936, Nam-gu was part of Dongnae County. A branch office called Daeyeon was set up in 1953, and in 1975 it became Nam-gu of Busan, then a directly governed city (Jikhalsi). In 1995, Suyeong-gu was split off from Nam-gu.

Nam-gu is where the East Sea and the South Sea meet. The Oryukdo Islands are used as the dividing point between the two seas. The foot of Hwangnyeongsan Mountain reaches the shore. There are Igidae Park, which has beautiful sea views, and Sinseondae Recreation Area. Sinseondae, Uam, and Gamman have container piers, so many places connected to port work are gathered there.

paras: Buk-gu was newly created in 1978 as Buk-gu of Busan, then a directly governed city (Jikhalsi). Before that, it was Gupo-eup in Dongnae County, and from 1963 it was the Gupo branch office of Busanjin-gu. Gangseo-gu was split off from Buk-gu in 1989, and Sasang-gu in 1995.

A story about a turtle is told about the name Gupo in Buk-gu. One ridge of Beombangsan Mountain is said to look like a turtle with a stone on its head, heading toward the Nakdonggang River (Nakdong River). There is also a story that warm air came out of a hole on the south side of the Namchang storehouse, which kept grain collected by the state, even in winter. People thought it was a place where a sea turtle slept through the winter. The Gupo ferry crossing was called Gamdongjin in the Joseon period, and it was widely known as the starting point of the Nakdong River waterway.

paras: The name Haeundae comes from 'Haeun', the courtesy name (ja, 字) of Choe Chi-won, a scholar of late Silla. The story says that he gave up his government post and was heading to Gayasan Mountain. He stopped at Haeundae, loved the view toward Dalmaji, and stayed. The story says he carved the three characters 'Haeundae' on a rock south of Dongbaekseom Island, and this became the place name. Haeundae started as the Haeundae branch office in 1953 and became Haeundae-gu in 1980.

Haeundae is where the South Sea and the East Sea divide. The land continues around Jangsan Mountain, and to the south the coast runs from Suyeong Bay to Songjeong Beach. It was designated a special tourism zone in 1994, and the Centum City industrial complex was built in Udong and Jaesong-dong in 2006.

paras: Saha-gu is at the southwestern end of Busan. In the Joseon period, it belonged to Dongnae in Gyeongsang Province. In 1910 it became Saha-myeon in Busan-bu (Busan Prefecture). In 1942 it joined the city of Busan and a Saha branch office was set up. In 1957 it was called the Saha branch office of Seo-gu, Busan, and in 1983 it was raised to Saha-gu.

Seo-gu is to the east, Sasang-gu is to the north, the Nakdonggang River (Nakdong River) flows to the west, and the South Sea is to the south. At the river mouth where the Nakdong River enters the sea, there is Eulsukdo Island, formed by soil carried by the river. Reed fields stretch without end. Many migratory birds visit, and there is a migratory bird habitat designated as Natural Monument No. 179. On a wide sandy area by the Nakdong River, there is Dadaepo Beach.

paras: Geumjeong-gu is a district that was newly created in 1988 by splitting off from Dongnae-gu. A story is told about the name of Geumjeongsan Mountain, which shares its name with the district. There was a well on the mountaintop. The story says that a golden fish rode down on five-colored clouds and played there, so the mountain is called Geumjeongsan (Golden Well Mountain).

Beomeosa Temple, on the eastern slope of Geumjeongsan, was built in 678, in the reign of King Munmu of Silla, by the Great Monk Uisang. Geumjeongsanseong Fortress (Geumjeongsan Fortress) was built along the mountain ridge by people of Dongnae who had lived through the Imjin War (the Japanese invasions, 1592-1598), to prepare for future wars. The fortress wall that remains today is said to have been built in 1703, in the reign of King Sukjong. The Nopo-dong Tombs are burial sites from the middle of the 3rd century to the early 4th century, and they show how people in Busan lived at that time.

paras: Gangseo-gu is where the Nakdonggang River (Nakdong River) meets the sea. In the past it belonged to Gimhae County. In 1978 part of Gimhae County was brought into Buk-gu of Busan, and in 1983 the Gangseo branch office was set up. In 1989, Garak-myeon, Noksan-myeon, and Cheonga-myeon were joined to form Gangseo-gu.

The Nakdong River mouth is a place that many migratory birds visit. There is also the Myeongji Migratory Bird Observatory, where people can see the birds on the mudflats up close. Gadeokdo Island, the biggest island in Busan, has the Galmaetgil trail, where people can enjoy the sea and the forest together. It seems that people began to live there in earnest in 1544, in the reign of King Jungjong of Joseon, when Gadeokjin and Cheonseongjin (military camps) were set up. Gangseo-gu is also described as the old homeland of Gaya.

paras: The name Yeonje-gu was made by taking one syllable each: 'Yeon' from Yeonsan-dong and 'Je' from Geoje-dong. It is said that this area was the central town of the state of Geochilsan in the Samhan period. When the city of Busan began its district system on January 1, 1957, it became part of Dongnae-gu. On March 1, 1995, it was split off from Dongnae-gu and became a new district.

Geoje-dong was once a place with wide fields. A big embankment was built so that Geojecheon Stream, which crosses these fields, would not overflow. The place was called Geoje-ri, meaning 'village with an embankment', and later became Geoje-dong. About the name of Yeonsan-dong, one story says it comes from the many water lilies in the old marshland. Another says it comes from Geumnyeonsan Mountain. Both stories are told.

paras: The name Suyeong comes from the Gyeongsang Left Naval Commander's Headquarters (Gyeongsangjwado Sugunjeoldosayeong) that was here in the Joseon period. It was the headquarters of the navy that guarded the East Sea side during the Imjin War (the Japanese invasions, 1592-1598). The name Suyeong (水營) was made by taking one character each: 'su' (水) from 'sugun' (navy) and 'yeong' (營) from 'jeoldosayeong' (commander's headquarters). The area became part of Nam-gu in 1975, and on March 1, 1995, it was split off from Nam-gu and became Suyeong-gu.

Suyeong has national heritage such as Suyeong Yaryu (a mask dance drama), Jwasuyeong Eobangnori (a fishermen's folk game), the South Gate of Suyeongseong Fortress, and the Gomsol (an old black pine tree). The '25 Uiyongsa' (25 Righteous Warriors) honors 25 navy soldiers and residents who fought to the end here during the Imjin War and died in battle. A memorial service is held there every year at the end of the ninth lunar month. The district is south of Geumnyeonsan Mountain and touches the sea. It has Gwangalli Beach, Gwangan Bridge, and Millak Waterside Park.

paras: In the Joseon period, the Sasang area belonged to Sacheon-myeon in Dongnae-bu (Dongnae Prefecture). Sacheon-myeon was divided into an upper part and a lower part. The upper part was called Sasang-myeon, and the lower part was called Saha-myeon. In 1914 it became Sasang-myeon in Dongnae County. On March 1, 1995, Sasang-gu was created by taking Samnak-dong, Mora-dong, Deokpo-dong, Gwaebeop-dong, Gamjeon-dong, Jurye-dong, Hakjang-dong, and Eomgung-dong from Buk-gu.

Pieces of Gimhae-style pottery were found in the shell mounds of Mora-dong and Hakjang-dong. So people seem to have lived here since about 2,000 years ago. The Nakdonggang River (Nakdong River) flows to the west and mountains continue to the east. Between them lies a flat, triangle-shaped stretch of land. Streams such as Hakjangcheon, Samnakcheon, and Gamjeoncheon flow across the town.

paras: In the Silla period, Gijang-gun was called Gaphwayanggok. In 757, in the reign of King Gyeongdeok, the name was changed to Gijang. Gijang County Office says the name probably comes from the fact that this was an edge of the land touching the sea and also an important place for defense.

In the Joseon period, Gijang-hyeon (Gijang County) was abolished in 1599 and set up again in 1617. In 1895 it became Gijang-gun. In 1914 the county was abolished and joined to Dongnae County, and in 1973 it was merged into Yangsan County. In 1995 it became Gijang-gun again and joined Busan Metropolitan City. In 2015, Jeonggwan-myeon was raised to Jeonggwan-eup.

paras: Jung-gu is a district located around the middle of Daegu Metropolitan City. In the Joseon era, it belonged to the main office (Daegu Bonbu) of Daegu Dohobu (protectorate). In 1914, only the Daegu-myeon area, which matches today's Jung-gu, became Daegu-bu (Daegu City) in North Gyeongsang Province. When the ward system began on January 1, 1963, the Jungbu Branch Office and the Jongno Branch Office were joined to form Jung-gu of Daegu City.

Unlike the other districts of Daegu, Jung-gu has no mountains. It sits on low land in the middle of a wide area surrounded by mountains. Small hills such as Yeongwisan, Dongsan (Cheongnara-eondeok Hill), and Amisan (Namsan) are found here and there. Jung-gu is the center of finance and business in Daegu. In 1980, Namsan-dong and parts of Dabong-dong and Daemyeong-dong in Nam-gu were added to Jung-gu.

paras: The Dong-gu website says this area began in 1938 as the Eastern Branch Office of Daegu-bu (Daegu City). When the ward system began on January 1, 1963, the Eastern Branch Office became Dong-gu of Daegu City. On April 1, 1980, it was split into Dong-gu and Suseong-gu. On July 1, 1981, Daegu became a directly governed city, and the Ansim and Gongsan areas were added to Dong-gu. It became a self-governing district on May 1, 1988, and became Dong-gu of Daegu Metropolitan City on January 1, 1995.

The northern end of Dong-gu is the top of Palgongsan Mountain in Dohak-dong, and the western end is Dodeoksan Mountain in Deokgok-dong. A story is told that Sinam-dong got its name because it is a rocky place downstream of Sincheon Stream, a newly formed river.

paras: Seo-gu began on November 2, 1938, when the Western Branch Office of Daegu-bu (Daegu City) was set up. In 1949, it became the Western Branch Office of Daegu City, and on January 1, 1963, when the ward system began, it became Seo-gu. On January 1, 1988, when Dalseo-gu was newly created, all of Seongdang-dong and Seongseo, and part of Naedang-dong, went to Dalseo-gu. Seo-gu became a self-governing district on May 1 of that year.

An old story is told about the name Bisan-dong. Long ago, this area was an open field. A young bride was washing clothes when she saw a big mountain floating toward her like a cloud. She shouted, "A mountain is flying here!" and the mountain landed right there. It was called "Nalmoe" (the flying mountain), and this became the name Bisan-dong, they say.

paras: Nam-gu is a district in Daegu Metropolitan City. In the Silla era, the land of today's Nam-gu belonged to Suseong-gun (Suseong County), which served as the center of the Daegu area. The Southern Branch Office of Daegu City was set up in 1951, and when the ward system was first introduced in January 1963, it became Nam-gu. In 1981, Wolbae-eup of Dalseong-gun was added to Nam-gu, but it moved to Dalseo-gu in January 1988. The self-governing district system began on May 1 of that year.

The Nam-gu website says the name Daemyeong-dong came from Du Sa-chung, a general of Ming China. Du Sa-chung came to help Korea during the Imjin War (the Japanese invasions, 1592-1598) and stayed in Joseon. A story is told that he thought of his homeland, Ming, and named the neighborhood Daemyeong-dong. Deeper inside Apsan Park, there is also a temple called Eunjeoksa (Eunjeok Temple).

paras: Buk-gu began on November 2, 1938, when the Northern Branch Office of Daegu-bu (Daegu City) was newly set up. On January 1, 1963, the Buk-gu Branch Office was joined with Dongbyeon-dong and Seobyeon-dong of Gongsan-myeon, and it became Buk-gu. In 1981, when Daegu became a directly governed city, the Chilgok-eup area of Chilgok-gun (Chilgok County) was added to Buk-gu. It became a self-governing district on May 1, 1988.

The name Chilseong-dong came from dolmens (ancient stone tombs). Seven dolmens once stood here, and their shapes looked like the Big Dipper, so they were called Chilseong-bawi (Seven Stars Rocks). The village that grew around the rocks became Chilseong-dong. In Yeongyeong-dong, there was Yeongyeong Seowon (a Confucian academy) built in 1563. It was the first seowon in the Daegu area. To the west of it, there is also a beautiful rock called Hwaam.

paras: The Suseong-gu website says this land was Wihwa-gun (Wihwa County) in the Silla era. King Gyeongdeok renamed it Suchang-gun, and in the early Goryeo era it became Suseong-gun. The name Suseong was taken from the records and history of the old Suseong-hyeon (Suseong District). It is said that a field called Suseong-ya (today's Hwanggeum-dong and Dusan-dong) forms the center of the district. When it was newly separated from Dong-gu on April 1, 1980, it was given the name Suseong-gu.

On July 1, 1981, when Daegu became a directly governed city, the Gosan-myeon area of Gyeongsan-gun (Gyeongsan County) was added to Suseong-gu. In Beomeo-dong, there was a post station called Beomeo-yeok in the Joseon era. A story is told that the name Beomeo came from a mountain, where Beomeo Catholic Church stands today, that looks like a crucian carp opening its mouth. A stream flows below it, so it looked as if the fish were floating.

paras: Dalseo-gu was created on January 1, 1988. It opened with 14 administrative dongs, made by taking all of the Seongseo and Wolbae areas of Seo-gu and Nam-gu, plus parts of other areas. It became a self-governing district on May 1 of that year. The Dalseo-gu Council opened on April 15, 1991, and on January 1, 1995, its name changed to Dalseo-gu, Daegu Metropolitan City.

The Ipseok (standing stone) in Jincheon-dong was designated Historic Site No. 411, a national cultural heritage, in 1998. A prehistoric site park was built there in 2000. The name Duryu-dong is said to come from the round, spread-out shape of the mountain. A story is told that Dowon-dong was called Dowon-gol because its valley is deep and the scenery is beautiful, like Wuling Peach Blossom Land (Mureung Dowon) in China.

paras: The Dalseong-gun website says that in prehistoric times, towns named Dalguhwa, Dalgubeol, and Dalseong appeared. After the Silla era, the name changed to Dalguhwa-hyeon, Daegu-hyeon (Daegu District), and Daegu-gun (Daegu County). On March 1, 1914, the town area of Daegu-gun was separated to become Daegu-bu (Daegu City). All of the outer area was joined with Hyeonpung-gun (Hyeonpung County) to form Dalseong-gun.

In 1981, Seongseo-eup, Wolbae-eup, and Gongsan-myeon were moved into Daegu, which had become a directly governed city. On March 1, 1995, Dalseong-gun moved from North Gyeongsang Province into Daegu Metropolitan City. After that, Hwawon became an eup (town) in 1992, Nongong in 1996, and Dasa in 1997. Green land is well kept around Biseulsan Mountain and the Nakdonggang River. DGIST (Daegu Gyeongbuk Institute of Science and Technology) is also located here.

paras: Gunwi-gun is a county in Daegu Metropolitan City. In the Samhan era (the Three Han period), small states such as Yeodamguk and Sodeungbunguk of Jinhan are said to have existed here. In 757, in Unified Silla, when the names of counties and districts were changed, the area became Gunwi-hyeon, Hyoryeong-hyeon, and Burim-hyeon. In 1018, in the Goryeo era, these three places belonged to Sangju-mok (a large provincial district).

In 1914, when counties and townships were combined, Uiheung-gun (Uiheung County) was added to Gunwi-gun and its 8 townships came under Gunwi. In 1973, the Gwanghyeon area of Geumseong-myeon in Uiseong-gun (Uiseong County) was added to Gunwi-myeon, and in 1979, Gunwi-myeon was raised to Gunwi-eup (town). In 2021, Goro-myeon was renamed Samguk Yusa-myeon, after the Samguk Yusa (Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms). On July 1, 2023, Gunwi-gun changed from North Gyeongsang Province to Daegu Metropolitan City.

paras: Jemulpo-gu is a district that was created on July 1, 2026, when Incheon's administrative system changed. The Incheon city website says it combines the former Dong-gu and the inland part of the former Jung-gu (not including the Yeongjong area). The history page on the district office website says that the Dong-gu Office opened on January 1, 1968, and that Incheon became a directly governed city in 1981. The Dong-gu area became Dong-gu of Incheon Metropolitan City on January 1, 1995, and then became Jemulpo-gu on July 1, 2026.

The history page says that people called this area Michuhol (an old name of the Incheon area) in the Baekje period (an ancient kingdom). It also says that Incheon Port opened in 1883. The port opened because of the Korea-U.S. Treaty of Amity and Commerce, which was signed at Hwadojin (an old coastal fort). The district's flower is the royal azalea and its bird is the seagull. The district office says that Hwadojin is full of azaleas in bloom in May.

paras: Yeongjong-gu is a new district. It was created on July 1, 2026, when the administrative system changed and the old Jung-gu was split into Jemulpo-gu and Yeongjong-gu. It is in charge of Yeongjong-dong, Yeongjong 1-dong, Yeongjong 2-dong, Unseo 1-dong, Unseo 2-dong, and Yongyu-dong.

The district office's history page says that its beginning goes back to Michuhol (an old name of the Incheon area) in the Baekje period (an ancient kingdom). It says that the area was raised to Incheon Dohobu (protectorate) in 1460, under King Sejo of Joseon. Incheon's Jung-gu opened on January 1, 1968. On January 1, 1989, Yeongjong-myeon and Yongyu-myeon of Gyeonggi Province joined Jung-gu, and Yeongjong-dong and Yongyu-dong were created. The district office says that it will run the district in a way that fits Yeongjong International City, and that it will grow a city where living, culture, and tourism come together, as well as future industries based on the airport.

paras: Michuhol-gu opened as Nam-gu of Incheon on January 1, 1968. Part of Nam-gu was split off when Namdong-gu was created in 1988 and Yeonsu-gu was created on March 1, 1995. A law to change the name of Nam-gu was announced on March 20, 2018, and the district started as Michuhol-gu of Incheon Metropolitan City on July 1 of that year. The district office describes Michuhol (an old name of the Incheon area) as a historic place name of this area.

The district's symbol picture shows people holding hands and moving forward, with Munhaksan Mountain and Subongsan Mountain at the center. The mascot, Michu, is said to be based on Prince Biryu of Baekje (an ancient kingdom), the main figure of the Michuhol kingdom. The name Hagik-dong comes from the shape of the nearby mountains, which look like a crane spreading its wings.

paras: Yeonsu-gu was split off from Nam-gu of Incheon Metropolitan City on March 1, 1995. At first it was in charge of five neighborhoods: Okryeon, Seonhak, Yeonsu, Cheonghak, and Dongchun. As the population grew, Songdo-dong was divided several times from 2012, and now the district has 15 administrative dongs (neighborhoods).

The district office website guesses that people have lived here since the Neolithic Age (the New Stone Age). It says that the area around Munhaksan Mountain is said to have been the capital of Biryu Baekje (the Michuhol kingdom), which King Biryu is said to have founded. In the Joseon Dynasty, most of Yeonsu was part of Meonugeum-myeon of Incheon Dohobu (protectorate). The name was changed to Seo-myeon in 1906. When the gu system began in 1968, the area became part of Nam-gu, and in 1981 Incheon became a directly governed city.

paras: In 1914, Namdong-gu was Namdong-myeon of Bucheon-gun. It joined Incheon-bu on April 1, 1940, and in 1968 it became part of Nam-gu of Incheon. On January 1, 1988, it was created as Namdong-gu of Incheon, then a directly governed city. It became a self-governing district on May 1 of that year. When the city was renamed Incheon Metropolitan City on January 1, 1995, it became Namdong-gu of Incheon Metropolitan City.

The district office website describes Namdong-gu as a place where city and countryside exist together and that has great potential to grow. Manwolsan Mountain, Cheolmasan Mountain, and Geomasan Mountain are in the north and east, next to Bupyeong-gu. In the west, the district meets the sea, where Sorae Port is. Institutions such as the City Hall and the Office of Education are in this district, and so is Namdong Industrial Complex, a large factory area.

paras: Bupyeong is a place where farming culture grew around the wide fields of the Bupyeong Plain. The district office website says that it was called Jubuto-gun in the Three Kingdoms period under Goguryeo and Jangje-gun in the Unified Silla period. It says that it was raised to Bupyeong Dohobu (protectorate) in 1413. It became Bunae-myeon of Bucheon-gun in 1914 and joined Incheon-bu in 1940.

After the 1970s, industry grew and large apartment complexes were built, so the area grew quickly. Seo-gu was split off in 1988 and Gyeyang-gu in 1995. On March 1, 1995, the district's name was changed from Buk-gu to Bupyeong-gu. The district office describes the district as a green city where urban forests and parks fit in well along Cheolmasan Mountain and Manwolsan Mountain.

paras: Gyeyang-gu is in the northeast of Incheon. The district office website says that there are wide plains and streams around Gyeyangsan Mountain, so people seem to have lived here since prehistoric times. It also says that the area was the historic center of northeastern Incheon from the Three Kingdoms period to the Joseon Dynasty. Today the district has 12 dongs (neighborhoods). It has a lot of green space, and the district office describes it as a place where city and countryside are mixed.

In 1215, Gyeyang became Gyeyang Dohobu (protectorate) of Goryeo, and in 1413 its name was changed to Bupyeong Dohobu of Joseon. It became part of Bunae-myeon of Bucheon-gun in 1914 and joined Incheon-bu in 1940. Buk-gu of Incheon was created on January 1, 1968. In 1989, Gyeyang-myeon of Gimpo-gun became Gyeyang-dong of Buk-gu, and Gyeyang-gu was established on March 1, 1995.

paras: Seohae-gu was created on July 1, 2026. Geomdan-gu was split off from Seo-gu of Incheon Metropolitan City, and Seo-gu was renamed Seohae-gu. In the past, this area was called Seogot. The district office website says that this means a coast that stretches long to the west.

The history page says that the area was Jubuto-gun in the Three Kingdoms period and Jangje-gun in the Unified Silla period. It says that it belonged to Bupyeong Dohobu (protectorate) in the Joseon Dynasty. It became Seogot-myeon of Bucheon-gun in 1914 and Seogot-myeon of Incheon-bu on April 1, 1940. After being the Seogot Branch Office of Buk-gu in 1968, it was split off from Buk-gu in 1988 and became Seo-gu of Incheon, then a directly governed city. On March 1, 1995, Geomdan-myeon of Gimpo-gun in Gyeonggi Province was merged into Seo-gu.

paras: In the name Geomdan, the character geom (黔) means "black" and dan (丹) means "red." The name is said to come from the sight of the sky and the land turning dark red at sunset, because the west coast has tidal flats. On April 1, 1914, Geomdan-myeon, Nojang-myeon, and Masan-myeon of Gimpo-gun in Gyeonggi Province were merged into Geomdan-myeon.

On March 1, 1995, Geomdan-myeon of Gimpo-gun in Gyeonggi Province joined Seo-gu of Incheon Metropolitan City and became Geomdan-dong. After that, a large new town was built and the population grew quickly, so the area was divided into several dongs (neighborhoods). Today it has Geomdan-dong, Bullodaegok-dong, Wondang-dong, Dangha-dong, Oryuwanggil-dong, Majeon-dong, Ara 1-dong, and Ara 2-dong. On July 1, 2026, Geomdan-gu was split off from Seo-gu and started as a new district.

paras: Ganghwa is a county in Incheon Metropolitan City. The county office website says that Ganghwa was called Gapbigocha in the past and Hyeolgu-gun in the Goguryeo period. It was raised to Ganghwa-gun in 1232, in the Goryeo period. When the Mongols invaded, King Gojong moved the capital here, and the place was also called "Gangdo" (Capital Ganghwa).

In 1394, in the Joseon Dynasty, Ganghwa Dohobu (protectorate) was created, and in 1627 it was raised to Ganghwa Yusubu (a special regional government office). Gyodong-gun joined Ganghwa-gun in 1914. In 1995, Ganghwa moved from Gyeonggi Province to Incheon Metropolitan City, and today it has 1 eup (town) and 12 myeon (townships). At the top of Manisan Mountain, which is 472.1 m above sea level, there is Chamseongdan Altar. It is said that Dangun (the legendary founder of the first Korean state) held a ceremony to the sky there. A heavenly ceremony is held there every Gaecheonjeol (National Foundation Day, October 3).

paras: Ongjin-gun is a county with many islands in the West Sea (Yellow Sea). It has 7 myeon (townships) and 81 ri (villages). The county office website says that there are 134 islands in all, with 24 islands where people live and 110 islands where no one lives. Ongjin-hyeon was set up in 1018, in the Goryeo period. In 1896, when the whole country adopted the 13-province system, it became Ongjin-gun of Hwanghae Province.

On August 15, 1945, it joined Gyeonggi Province, and on July 1, 1973, six myeon (townships) of Bucheon-gun joined Ongjin-gun. After that, in 1989, Yeongjong-myeon and Yongyu-myeon moved to Incheon, a directly governed city, and in 1994 Daebu-myeon moved to Ansan-si in Gyeonggi Province. On March 1, 1995, Ongjin-gun was merged into Incheon Metropolitan City, and on July 20, 1999, Songnim-myeon was renamed Yeonpyeong-myeon.

paras: Dong-gu is the district on the east side of Daejeoncheon (Daejeon Stream). In the old days, it belonged to Usul-gun (Usul County) in the Baekje period and Bipung-gun (Bipung County) in the Silla period. During Goryeo and Joseon, most of it belonged to the Hoedeok area (Hoedeok-gogeul, a county town). In 1971, a branch office was set up in the east (Dongbu Chuljangso), and in 1977, Dong-gu was created east of Daejeoncheon and Jung-gu west of it.

In 1914, when Daejeon-gun (Daejeon County) was newly formed, Daejeon-myeon (Daejeon Township) took its place on what is now Dong-gu land, and this became the start of today's Daejeon. In the 1940s and 1950s, shops gathered around Daejeon Station, and Dong-gu rose as an important part of Daejeon. In 1989, Daejeon became a directly governed city (Jikhalsi), and Dong-gu became a self-governing district. In the east there is Daecheongho Lake, which has beautiful scenery.

paras: Jung-gu is the district in the center of Daejeon. In 1977, Jung-gu was created by joining the land handled by the Jungbu and Seobu branch offices (Jungbu Chuljangso and Seobu Chuljangso). In 1988, Seo-gu was created, and places such as Boksu-dong and Doma-dong were split off from Jung-gu. In 1989, Daejeon became a directly governed city (Jikhalsi), and Jung-gu became a self-governing district too.

The highest mountain in Jung-gu is Bomunsan Mountain, which is 458 m high. The ridge of Bomunsan runs through Daeheung-dong, Seonhwa-dong, Yongdu-dong, and Mok-dong, and then is cut off by Yudeungcheon (Yudeung Stream). The low hill in Yongdu-dong divides Daejeon into east and west. Daejeoncheon (Daejeon Stream) flows on the east side and Yudeungcheon on the west side, and they separate Jung-gu from its neighboring districts. In 1997, Ppuri Park (Root Park) opened in Chimsan-dong.

paras: The land of Seo-gu was the Seobu Branch Office of Daejeon (Seobu Chuljangso) in 1971. In 1977, it belonged to Jung-gu, and in 1988, it became Seo-gu. In 1989, Giseong-myeon (Giseong Township) of Daedeok-gun (Daedeok County) joined Seo-gu. In the 1990s, neighborhoods such as Samcheon-dong, Jeongnim-dong, Tanbang-dong, Dunsan-dong, and Wolpyeong-dong were split off one after another and newly created. In 2022, Doan-dong was split off from Gasuwon-dong.

Seo-gu lies between Yuseong-gu, Daedeok-gu, and Jung-gu. It is centered on Gubongsan Mountain and Wolpyeongsan Mountain, with Gapcheon (Gap Stream) and Yudeungcheon (Yudeung Stream) flowing around it. Except for the mountains in the southwest, the land is low and flat, and it is described as fertile. Gasuwon and Giseong are rural areas, Doma-dong and Byeon-dong are the old downtown, and Dunsan is the new downtown.

paras: People are said to have lived in Yuseong since very early times. In the Samhan period, Sinheunguk (Sinheun State), one of the tribal states of Mahan, is known to have been on Bingyesan Mountain, between Gyesan-dong and Hakha-dong. In 1935, the area became part of Daedeok-gun (Daedeok County), and in 1973, Yuseong-myeon (Yuseong Township) was raised to Yuseong-eup (Yuseong Town).

In 1983, the land of Yuseong-eup was placed under the Yuseong Branch Office (Yuseong Chuljangso), which was run by Jung-gu of Daejeon. In 1984, this branch office was raised to be directly under the city of Daejeon. In 1989, when Daejeon became a directly governed city (Jikhalsi), Yuseong-gu was newly created. In 1992, the district office was moved from Jangdae-dong to Eoeun-dong. In 1994, five tourist areas across the country, including Yuseong-gu, were designated by the government as special tourism zones (Gwangwang Teukgu).

sources.t: Yuseong-gu Office, Major history

paras: Daedeok-gu is in the northeast of Daejeon, and it borders Chungcheongbuk-do (North Chungcheong Province) on the north and east. It was a main part of the old Hoedeok-hyeon (Hoedeok, an old local district). In 1413, during the reign of King Taejong of Joseon, it was given the name Hoedeok-gun. In 1935, Daedeok-gun (Daedeok County) was created from the rest of the land, apart from Daejeon-bu (Daejeon Town). In 1989, Daedeok-gun joined Daejeon, a directly governed city (Jikhalsi), and Daedeok-gu was created.

Daedeok-gu has Gyejoksan Mountain and Daecheongho Lake. It also has cultural heritage sites such as Hoedeok Hyanggyo (Hoedeok Confucian school), Dongchundang (Dongchundang House), and Gyejoksanseong (Gyejoksan Fortress). The Hoedeok Junction, where the Gyeongbu Expressway and the Honam Expressway meet, makes it a crossroads of traffic linking the Yeongnam and Honam regions. The district also has Daejeon Industrial Complex and Daedeok Industrial Complex. In Yongho-dong, there is a site from about 100,000 years ago, and it is the oldest site in Daejeon.

paras: Jung-gu was part of Jinhan, one of the Three Han states, and a village called Gurahwa-chon is said to have formed here. In the time of King Pasa of Silla, Gurahwa-hyeon (Gurahwa County) was set up. In 995, under King Seongjong of Goryeo, it was given another name, Hakseong ("Crane Fortress"). In 1413 in Joseon it became Ulsan-gun (Ulsan County), and in 1599 it became Ulsan Dohobu (Ulsan Protectorate). It became Ulsan City in 1962. In 1985 the city started a ward system, and the Jung-gu Office opened.

The Taehwagang River (Taehwa River) flows through Jung-gu. The district also has Sipridaebat (Sipri Bamboo Grove), one of the 12 scenic sights of Ulsan, so its symbolic tree is bamboo. As the place name Hakseong shows, Jung-gu is described as a land of cranes from long ago. In 1997, Jung-gu of Ulsan Metropolitan City started as an autonomous district.

paras: Nam-gu was part of Jinhan, one of the Three Han states, and it was Gurahwa-hyeon (Gurahwa County) in the Three Kingdoms period. It was first set as Ulju in the Goryeo period, and it belonged to Ulsan-gun (Ulsan County) in Joseon. When Ulsan became a city in 1962, the Jangsaengpo Branch Office was set up. In 1985 the city started a ward system and Nam-gu opened, and in 1997 it became Nam-gu of Ulsan Metropolitan City.

The names of the neighborhoods in Nam-gu hold stories. For Mugeo-dong, a story says that a boy monk who was guiding King Gyeongsun of Silla disappeared without a trace. Samsan-dong is said to be named for three mountain peaks. Yongyeon-dong is said to be named because a dragon lived in Garimot (Gari Pond). Jangsaengpo-dong is said to be named either because the port was thin and long, or because it was a port with jangseung (wooden village guardian posts).

paras: In 1910, Dong-gu was called Dong-myeon (East Township) of Ulsan-gun (Ulsan County), and in 1936 it became Bangeojin-eup (Bangeojin Town). When Ulsan became a city in 1962, it came under the Bangeojin Branch Office. In 1988 the Bangeojin Branch Office was raised to the Dong-gu Office. In 1997, Dong-gu of Ulsan Metropolitan City started as an autonomous district. Yeompo-dong moved from Jung-gu to Dong-gu that year, and then moved to Buk-gu the next year.

The symbolic tree of Dong-gu is the gomsol (Japanese black pine). It grows widely at Daewangam Park and Jujeon Beach, and it is said to stay green all year and to be very strong. The symbolic flower is the dongbaek (camellia), which blooms red from December to March. The symbolic bird is the seagull, a common sight on the coast, and it is said to be a symbol of hope for sailors.

paras: The land of Buk-gu was the area of Gurahwa-hyeon (Gurahwa County) and Yulpo-hyeon (Yulpo County) in Silla. In 757, under King Gyeongdeok, the names of these counties were changed to Hagok-hyeon and Dongjin-hyeon. In 1413, under King Taejong of Joseon, Ulju was renamed Ulsan, and this is when the name "Ulsan" first appeared. In 1914, when the local system was redone, Nongso-myeon, Gangdong-myeon, Hasang-myeon and Dong-myeon (townships) were created.

Ulsan Metropolitan City started in 1997. Buk-gu was formed by joining Jinjang-dong, Hyomun-dong, Songjeong-dong and Yangjeong-dong of Jung-gu with Nongso-eup (Nongso Town) and Gangdong-myeon (Gangdong Township) of Ulju-gu. The next year, Yeompo-dong of Dong-gu also joined Buk-gu. One of the 12 scenic sights of Buk-gu is the Cheonmasan Hinoki Cypress Forest Bathing Area. The symbolic flower of the district is the tiger lily, the tree is the zelkova, and the bird is the blue magpie.

paras: Ulju-gun was land of Jinhan, one of the Three Han states. In 1018, under King Hyeonjong of Goryeo, it was given the name Ulju. In 1413, under King Taejong of Joseon, it became Ulsan-gun (Ulsan County). In 1914, Eonyang-gun (Eonyang County) was joined to Ulsan-gun. When Ulsan became a city in 1962, Ulsan-gun changed its name to Ulju-gun.

In 1995, Ulsan City and Ulsan-gun were joined, and Ulju-gu was formed. In 1997, Ulsan became a metropolitan city, and Ulju-gu became Ulju-gun. The county office website introduces the Bangudae Petroglyphs and the Cheonjeon-ri Inscriptions and Petroglyphs as the rock carvings that represent Ulju-gun. A page that introduces the county's characters says that Ganjeolgot (Ganjeolgot Point) is the place where the sun rises first in the New Year in Northeast Asia.

paras: Sejong-si is in the middle of the Chungcheong region. To the east is Cheongju-si in North Chungcheong Province. To the west is Gongju-si in South Chungcheong Province. To the south is Daejeon, and to the north is Cheonan-si in South Chungcheong Province. The area first appears in the Samguk Sagi (History of the Three Kingdoms) under the names Duingji-hyeon (Duingji County) and Guji-hyeon (Guji County) of Baekje. Paleolithic tools have also been found along the Geumgang River (Geum River), so people are thought to have lived here much earlier.

In 757, when place names across the country were changed to Chinese characters, Duingji-hyeon became Yeongi-hyeon (Yeongi County) and Guji-hyeon became Geumji-hyeon (Geumji County). In 940, Geumji-hyeon was renamed Jeonui-hyeon (Jeonui County). In 1914, Yeongi-gun (Yeongi County) and Jeonui-gun (Jeonui County) were joined with part of Gongju's land to become Yeongi-gun. On July 1, 2012, Sejong Special Self-Governing City officially opened.

paras: The name Suwon (水原) has 'water' in it. Suwon City Hall explains that in the old name Maehol, 'mae' is thought to mean 'water' and 'hol' to mean 'town', and that the names Suseong, Suju and Suwon can all be seen as coming from 'water town'. It was raised to Suju in 940, early in the Goryeo period (Goryeo Dynasty). The name 'Suwon' first appeared in 1271, under King Wonjong, when Suwon Dohobu (protectorate) was set up.

In 1789, under King Jeongjo, the center of Suwon-bu (Suwon Prefecture) was moved to a new place. In 1793 the new center was named 'Hwaseong' and raised to Hwaseong Yusubu (a special prefecture led by a governor called a yusu). In 1796 the construction of Hwaseong was finished. Suwon became Suwon-gun (Suwon County) in 1895, and then Suwon-si (Suwon City) on August 15, 1949.

paras: The Jangan-gu Office opened on July 1, 1988. The name Jangan comes from Janganmun (Jangan Gate), the north gate among the four main gates of Suwon Hwaseong (Hwaseong Fortress). It is said that King Jeongjo gave this name to bring back to Hwaseong the glory of Chang'an (Jangan in Korean), an old capital of China. In 1993 and 2003, some neighborhoods (dong) were moved to Paldal-gu.

The district office describes the district as lying at the foot of Gwanggyosan (Mt. Gwanggyo). It has cultural heritage of Hwaseong such as Janganmun and Banghwasuryujeong (Banghwasuryu Pavilion). It also has Gwanggyo Park and Manseok Park. Sungkyunkwan University, the Gyeonggi Provincial Office of Education and the Gyeonggi Provincial Police Agency are here too.
