paras: Yeongyang was called Goeun in early Silla, and the name Yeongyang was added toward the end of that period. In 1179, during Goryeo, Yeongyang-hyeon was newly created. It was abolished twice in the Joseon period, but in 1683 the local people asked again and it was brought back. In 1895, it became Yeongyang-gun, and in 1914, Ipam-myeon and Seokbo-myeon joined Yeongyang-gun.

Ilwolsan Mountain is 1,219 m above sea level, and it is where Banbyeoncheon Stream begins. Yeongyang-gun presents Eumsik Dimibang, a cookbook written in Hangul (the Korean alphabet) more than 350 years ago, as a tourist resource. Its main crops are chili peppers, apples, wild mountain greens, and cheongung (a medicinal herb). It also introduces the stories of literary figures such as Jo Ji-hun, O Il-do, and Yi Byeong-gak.

paras: Yeongdeok was called Yasiheol in the Three Kingdoms period, and after Silla unified the three kingdoms, it became Yaseong-gun. In early Goryeo, the name changed to Yeongdeok. In 1415, the 15th year of King Taejong of Joseon, a jihyeonsa (a local official post) was set up. Yeonghae, which later joined Yeongdeok, was called Usi-guk in the Samhan period. It is said that when Goryeo's King Taejo first visited, the people were polite and had a custom of giving way to each other, so he called it Yeju.

Yeongdeok-gun was originally two counties, Yeongdeok and Yeonghae, which were joined in 1914. In 1979, Yeongdeok-myeon became Yeongdeok-eup (a town). It lies in the northeast of North Gyeongsang Province and borders Pohang-si, Uljin-gun, Yeongyang-gun, and Cheongsong-gun. The Taebaek Mountains stretch to the southeast and wrap around Yeongdeok, and it is written that Osipcheon Stream has been a lifeline for the people here.

paras: Cheongdo was Uyu-guk in the Samhan period and was later absorbed by Silla. From the time of King Yurye in 280, it was called Iseo-guk, and in 1018, the 9th year of Goryeo's King Hyeonjong, it took the name Cheongdo-gun. In 1949, Cheongdo-myeon became Cheongdo-eup (a town), and in 1979, Hwayang-myeon became Hwayang-eup.

Cheongdo-gun is in the far south of North Gyeongsang Province. It is a transport hub, with the Gyeongbu Line railway, an expressway, and national roads passing through. The county describes its land as good for growing grains and fruits of every kind and as the best place in the province for raising fruit trees. It also says that the Hwarang spirit (the spirit of Silla's young warriors) and the Saemaul Undong (New Village Movement) began here. In October, the Cheongdo Bansi Festival (a festival of flat persimmons) is held.

paras: The county office website says that Goryeong is where King Ijinasi founded Daegaya in 42. In 562, Silla's King Jinheung absorbed Daegaya and made it Daegaya-gun, and in 757, under King Gyeongdeok, it got the name Goryeong-gun.

In 1413, in the Joseon period, a hyeongam (a local government official) was placed there, and in 1895, Goryeong-hyeon became Goryeong-gun. In 1930, Ssangdong-myeon and Imcheon-myeon were joined to form Ssangnim-myeon. In 1979, Goryeong-myeon was raised to an eup (a town), and in 2015, Goryeong-eup was renamed Daegaya-eup.

paras: The county office website says that Seongju grew into Seongsan Gaya around the 4th century. In 757, the 16th year of Silla's King Gyeongdeok, Bonpi-hyeon was renamed Sinan-hyeon, and in 940, the 23rd year of Goryeo's King Taejo, it was raised to Gyeongsan-bu. The Seongju-gun website writes that the land is mostly round in shape, with a plain made by the Nakdong River and its tributaries in the northwest.

In 1308, the 34th year of King Chungnyeol, it was raised to Seongju-mok. The county office website says the name Seongju was first used at that time. In 1895, it became Seongju-gun, and in 1979, Seongju-myeon was raised to an eup (a town). In August 2024, Geumsu-myeon was renamed Geumsugangsan-myeon.

paras: Chilgok is a name that means "seven valleys." Gasan, the famous mountain of Palgeo-hyeon, is also called Chilbongsan. It is said that the name comes from seven low peaks surrounding the top and seven valleys on all sides. In 1640, Gasan Fortress was built and a dohobu (protectorate) was set up, and the name Chilgok began to be used.

In 1895, it became Chilgok-gun. In 1914, Indong-gun and Yangmok-myeon were joined to it, and the county office moved to Waegwan. In 1949, Waegwan-myeon became Waegwan-eup (a town). Chilgok-gun describes itself as a land of defending the nation, with sites of the Battle of the Nakdong River and the Battle of Dabu-dong from the Korean War, and Gasan Fortress.

paras: In Yecheon, dolmens and menhirs (standing stones) from prehistoric times have been found, and there is a northern-style dolmen in Sanggeumgok-ri, Yongmun-myeon. The name "Suju-chon" appears in the Samguk Sagi (History of the Three Kingdoms) in the time of Silla's King Nulji, and in 757 it became Yecheon-gun. In 935, under Goryeo's King Taejo, it became Boju. In 1172, under King Myeongjong, it was changed to Giyang, and in 1204 it went back to Boju.

In the time of King Taejong of Joseon, it became Bocheon-gun, and in 1416 the old name Yecheon was brought back. In 1914, Yonggung-gun was joined to it. In 2016, Sangni-myeon was renamed Hyoja-myeon, and Hari-myeon was renamed Eunpung-myeon. In February 2024, Homyeong-myeon became Homyeong-eup (a town).

paras: Bonghwa-gun is at the northern end of North Gyeongsang Province. It borders Uljin-gun and Yeongyang-gun to the east, Andong-si to the south, and Yeongju-si to the west. To the north, it borders Yeongwol-gun and Taebaek-si in Gangwon Special Self-Governing Province. In 1895, Bonghwa-hyeon was renamed Bonghwa-gun.

In the Samhan period, Bonghwa belonged to Gijeo-guk of Jinhan, and in the time of Goryeo's King Hyeonjong, it was given the name Bongseong-hyeon. In 1979, Bonghwa-myeon was raised to Bonghwa-eup (a town). The Bonghwa-gun website says that it has many mountains and little flat land.

paras: Uljin is at the northeastern end of North Gyeongsang Province. It faces the East Sea, and people there do farming and fishing together. Long ago, there was a small country called Ujung-guk in the Jinhan confederation. Under Goguryeo's King Jangsu, it briefly became Goguryeo land. In 757, under Silla's King Gyeongdeok, Ujinya-hyeon was renamed Uljin-gun.

Around 940, under Goryeo's King Taejo, it became Uljin-hyeon and a hyeollyeong (a county magistrate) was placed there. From early Goryeo, it also governed Ulleungdo Island. In 1914, Uljin-gun and Pyeonghae-gun were joined to become Uljin-gun. Uljin-gun had belonged to Gangwon-do, and in 1963 it became part of North Gyeongsang Province. In 2015, Seo-myeon was renamed Geumgangsong-myeon, and Wonnam-myeon was renamed Maehwa-myeon.

paras: It is said that people began living on Ulleungdo Island around the Bronze Age or the Iron Age. In 512, the Silla general Isabu conquered Usan-guk, and this is when Ulleungdo first appears in books. People began to move to the island in 1883, and in 1900, Ulleungdo became Uldo-gun and belonged to Gangwon-do.

Uldo-gun was moved into South Gyeongsang Province in 1906 and into North Gyeongsang Province in 1914, and in 1949 it became Ulleung-gun again. In 1979, Nam-myeon became Ulleung-eup (a town), which made the present one eup and two myeon. The eastern end of the county is Dongdo (East Islet) of Dokdo, and in 2000, Dokdo-ri was newly created in Ulleung-eup.

paras: In 1408, during the Joseon era, the towns of Uichang and Hoewon were joined under the new name 'Changwon' and raised to the rank of a bu (prefecture). In 1980, Changwon-si was newly created, and in 1983 the Gyeongnam provincial office moved to Changwon. On July 1, 2010, Changwon-si, Masan-si, and Jinhae-si merged into one, and today's Changwon-si began.

The merged Changwon-si is divided into Uichang-gu, Seongsan-gu, Masanhappo-gu, Masanhoewon-gu, and Jinhae-gu. On January 13, 2022, it became a special-case city (teukrye-si). Changwon lies in the southern part of central Gyeongsangnam-do. Masan Bay and Jinhae Bay extend to its south. The city office describes it as the center of industry and the economy in central Gyeongnam, with a large machinery industrial complex.

paras: Changwon-si Uichang-gu opened on July 1, 2010, when the merged Changwon-si began. The name Changwon came in the 8th year of King Taejong of Joseon (1408), when the two towns of Uichang and Hoewon were joined. It is said to take the 'chang' from Uichang and the 'won' from Hoewon. Uichang began as Uian-gun (Uian County) in the Silla era and was raised to Uichang in the 8th year of King Chungnyeol of Goryeo (1282).

It is described as the root of Changwon, because the town wall of Changwon-bu (Changwon Prefecture) stood here. It is a center of industry, with the Changwon National Industrial Complex and a technopark. On the farmland along the Nakdong River, crops such as sweet persimmons, watermelons, and paprika are grown. It is a district where city and countryside lie together.

paras: Changwon-si Seongsan-gu opened on July 1, 2010, when districts were created in Changwon-si. Seongsan is a Chinese-character name meaning 'a mountain with a fortress,' and it refers to a hill in Naedong inside the district. On July 1, 2021, the borders with Uichang-gu were redrawn, and areas such as Yongji-dong came into Seongsan-gu.

The district has Seongsan Shell Mound (Historic Site No. 240), Seongjusa Temple, built in the Silla era, and Bulgoksa Temple, built in the Goryeo era. It also has the Changwon National Industrial Complex, the center of Korea's machinery industry. In Sangnam-dong and Jungang-dong, banks and large shopping areas are gathered. Changwon Arboretum is the 3rd public arboretum in Gyeongsangnam-do.

paras: Changwon-si Masanhappo-gu opened in 2010, when Masan, Changwon, and Jinhae merged into the new Changwon-si. Its name was taken from an old place name. In the Three Kingdoms era it was Golpo-guk (Golpo State), and in 757, in Unified Silla, it became Happo-hyeon (Happo County). There was also a Happo-gu in 1990, but it was abolished on December 31, 2000.

New things came into this area after Masan Port opened on May 1, 1899. It is also a center of the democracy movement that led the March 15 Uprising. Masan Fish Market is a market for farm and sea products with a tradition of more than 250 years. The district also has Mount Muhak, the Masan Museum, and the Moon Shin Art Museum.

paras: Changwon-si Masanhoewon-gu is a district newly created on July 1, 2010, when the merged Changwon-si began. There was also a Hoewon-gu in Masan-si in 1990, but it was abolished on December 31, 2000. Hoewon is an old name of Masan. In the 2010 merger, the old place name was kept, and the northern part of Masan was named Masanhoewon-gu.

Mountains such as Mount Muhak, Mount Cheonju, and Mount Pallyong blend into the city. With the Naeseo, Seomasan, and Dongmasan interchanges and KTX Masan Station, it is a place where roads meet. The district has the March 15 National Cemetery, Changshin University, and Masan Baseball Stadium. It also has the Bongam and Jungni industrial complexes.

paras: Changwon-si Jinhae-gu opened on July 1, 2010, when the merged Changwon-si began. The name Jinhae was first used in 1912, when it became Jinhae-myeon (Jinhae Township). It became Jinhae-eup (Jinhae Town) in 1931 and Jinhae-si on September 1, 1955. Ungcheon joined Jinhae-si in 1973, and Ungdong joined in 1983.

The district office says it will build on the beautiful coastline and the largest cherry blossom festival in Korea, and grow into a center of sea tourism and leisure. A new port is being built and new development projects are under way, so the district is said to have great potential to grow. The Ungcheon and Ungdong area of Jinhae-gu was once Ungcheon-hyeon (Ungcheon County). In 1452, a new county was made by joining Ungsin-hyeon, Wanpo-hyeon, and Cheoneupbugok.

paras: Jinju is said to have been the old capital of Goryeong Gaya (a Gaya state). In 940, in the 23rd year of King Taejo of Goryeo, it first got the name 'Jinju.' In 983, it became one of the twelve large towns in the country called mok (Jinju-mok). In 1896 it became the seat of the Gyeongsangnam-do provincial office and the center of Gyeongnam's government. On April 1, 1925, the provincial office moved to Busan.

When local self-government began on August 15, 1948, Jinju-bu (Jinju Prefecture) was raised to Jinju-si. On January 1, 1995, Jinju-si and Jinyang-gun (Jinyang County) merged into one. The city office describes Jinju as a city of history and tradition, with the Battle of Jinju (1592), Jinjuseong Fortress, Chokseongnu Pavilion, and the Namgang River. It also describes Jinju as a UNESCO Creative City in the field of Crafts and Folk Art, and a festival city that hosts the Jinju Namgang Yudeung Festival (Lantern Festival) and the Gaecheon Arts Festival.

paras: The name Tongyeong is a short form of 'Samdo Sugun Tongjeyeong' (Joint Naval Command of the Three Provinces). In 1593, the first Samdo Sugun Tongjeyeong was set up on Hansando Island. In 1604, Naval Commander Yi Gyeong-jun moved it to Duryongpo (today's Tongyeong-si), and that is how the name Tongyeong began. The Tongjeyeong was abolished in 1895.

In 1914, Yongnam-gun (Yongnam County) and Geoje-gun (Geoje County) were joined to become Tongyeong-gun (Tongyeong County), and in 1931, Tongyeong-myeon (Tongyeong Township) became Tongyeong-eup (Tongyeong Town). On September 1, 1955, Tongyeong-eup was raised to a city and named 'Chungmu-si,' after the name Chungmu-gong. On January 1, 1995, Chungmu-si and Tongyeong-gun merged into one, creating Tongyeong-si, where city and countryside lie together.

paras: Sacheon City Hall says the name Sacheon came from the old name 'Samul.' Samul changed to Sasu and Saju, and in 1413, in the 13th year of King Taejong of Joseon, it became Sacheon. The city hall guesses that the name Samul came from the meaning 'a beautiful place surrounded by water on all sides.'

In 1415, Sacheonjin (Sacheon Fort) was set up to stop Japanese pirates. In 1895, it became Sacheon-gun (Sacheon County) of Jinju-bu. In 1931, Samcheonpo-myeon (Samcheonpo Township) became Samcheonpo-eup (Samcheonpo Town). On July 8, 1956, Samcheonpo-eup and Namyang-myeon merged to become Samcheonpo-si. On May 10, 1995, Samcheonpo-si and Sacheon-gun merged to become today's Sacheon-si.

paras: Gimhae is where King Suro founded Garak-guk (also called Geumgwan Gaya) in the year 42. In 532 it was joined to Silla and became Geumgwan-gun (Geumgwan County). In 756 it became Gimhae-sogyeong, a secondary capital of Unified Silla. In 971, in the Goryeo era, its name changed to Gimhae-bu (Gimhae Prefecture).

In 1895 it became Gimhae-gun (Gimhae County), and on November 1, 1931, Gimhae-myeon (Gimhae Township) became Gimhae-eup (Gimhae Town). In 1978, parts such as Daejeo-eup went into Busan. On July 1, 1981, Gimhae-eup was raised to Gimhae-si. In 1989, Garak-myeon and Noksan-myeon also went into Busan. On May 10, 1995, Gimhae-si and Gimhae-gun merged to become today's Gimhae-si. On July 1, 2013, Jangyu-myeon was divided into Jangyu 1-dong, 2-dong, and 3-dong.

paras: Miryang is thought to have been a small state called 'Mirimidong-guk' in the Samhan era. In 505, in the 6th year of King Jijeung of Silla, Mirimidong-guk was joined to Silla and Chuhwa-gun (Chuhwa County) was set up. In 757 it became Milseong-gun (Milseong County), and in 995, in the 14th year of King Seongjong of Goryeo, it was raised to Milju-gun (Milju County). In 1390, in the 2nd year of King Gongyang of Goryeo, it became Miryang-bu (Miryang Prefecture), and in 1415, in the Joseon era, it became Miryang-dohobu (Miryang Protectorate).

In 1896 it became Miryang-gun (Miryang County) of Gyeongsangnam-do, and in 1931 Miryang-myeon (Miryang Township) became Miryang-eup (Miryang Town). In 1963, Samnangjin-myeon was raised to Samnangjin-eup, and in 1973, Hanam-myeon was raised to Hanam-eup. On January 1, 1989, Miryang-eup was raised to Miryang-si and separated from Miryang-gun. On January 1, 1995, Miryang-si and Miryang-gun merged to become today's Miryang-si.

paras: In Geoje, a town called Sanggun was created in 677 (the 17th year of King Munmu). In 757 (the 16th year of King Gyeongdeok), its name changed to Geoje-gun (Geoje County). In the Joseon era, in 1414, it was joined with Geochang to become Jechang-hyeon (Jechang County), and it was separated again the next year. In 1592, during the Imjin War (the Japanese invasions, 1592-1598), the Joseon navy led by Admiral Yi Sun-sin won its first victory in Okpo Bay (the Battle of Okpo).

In 1951, after the Korean War began, the UN Forces' No. 1 Prisoner of War Camp was set up in many parts of Geoje, such as Gohyeon and Suwol. The Geoje Bridge opened on April 8, 1971. In 1973 and 1974, shipyard construction began in Okpo and Jukdo. On January 1, 1995, Jangseungpo-si and Geoje-gun merged to become today's Geoje-si. On December 14, 2010, the Geoga Bridge opened.

paras: In the 5th year of King Munmu of Silla, Yangsan was called Samnyangju. In 757 it was called Yangju (良州), and in 940, the 23rd year of King Taejo of Goryeo, it became Yangju (梁州) with a different Chinese character. The present name "Yangsan" came in 1413, the 13th year of King Taejong of Joseon, when it was named Yangsan-gun (梁山郡). In 1896 it became part of Gyeongsangnam-do (South Gyeongsang Province).

In 1973, six myeon (townships) of Dongnae-gun (Gijang, Ilgwang, Jangan, Seosaeng, Jeonggwan and Cheolma) were added to Yangsan-gun. In 1979, Yangsan-myeon became an eup (town). In 1995, the two eup of Gijang and Jangan and the three myeon of Ilgwang, Jeonggwan and Cheolma moved to Gijang-gun in Busan Metropolitan City. On March 1, 1996, Yangsan-gun became Yangsan-si. On April 1, 2007, Ungsang-eup was divided into four dong (neighborhoods).

paras: Uiryeong-gun is in Gyeongsangnam-do, where the Nakdonggang River (Nakdong River) meets its branch, the Namgang River (Nam River). In 685, in the Unified Silla period, it was called Jangham-hyeon. In 757 the name changed to Uiryeong-hyeon. In 1895 it became Uiryeong-gun in Jinju-bu (Jinju Prefecture), and the next year, 1896, it became Uiryeong-gun in Gyeongsangnam-do.

In the northwest, Jagulsan Mountain, 897 m above sea level, rises high. In the east, the Nakdonggang River separates it from Changnyeong-gun. To honor Gwak Jae-u and the righteous army (uibyeong, volunteer fighters), the people of Uiryeong built the Uibyeong Tower (Righteous Army Tower) at the foot of Namsan Hill in Uiryeong-eup in 1972. Since 1973, they have held the Uibyeong Festival on April 22. In 1979, Uiryeong-myeon became an eup, so the county now has 1 eup and 12 myeon.

paras: Haman-gun is where Byeonjin Anyaguk (a state of Byeonhan) stood in the Samhan period. In the Gaya period it was the home of Aragaya, one of the six Gaya states. During the reign of King Beopheung of Silla, it was joined to Silla and became Asiryang-gun. In 757 it was renamed Haman-gun. The Haman County Office says Anyaguk was probably widely known, since long ago, for trade by sea between the Chinese commanderies and counties and other regions.

In the Goryeo period, Hamju was set up in 995 and raised to a gun (county) in 1373. In the Joseon period, it was raised to a dohobu (protectorate) in 1506. In 1979, Gaya-myeon became an eup. Chilwon was a separate town from Haman until 1906. In January 2015, Chilwon-myeon became an eup.

paras: The oldest record of Changnyeong is Bulsaguk, which appears in the Records of the Three Kingdoms (a Chinese history book) around the 1st century. In the Gaya period it was a state called Bulsaguk or Bihwagaya, and it was joined to Silla early on. In 940, the 23rd year of King Taejo of Goryeo, the name Hwawang-gun was changed to the present "Changnyeong". In 1914, Yeongsan-gun was merged into Changnyeong-gun, and it has stayed this way to the present.

The east has many mountains, and the west, along the Nakdonggang River, has rich farmland. It grows crops such as onions, garlic, red peppers and sweet persimmons, so it is a typical farming area. The Jungbu Naeryuk Expressway (Central Inland Expressway) and national roads pass through, so travel is also easy. The county office says there are many places to see, such as Bugok Hot Springs, Hwawangsan Mountain and Upo Wetland.

paras: Goseong has an island area where pottery was found in a Neolithic shell mound. It is also a place named in the Records of the Three Kingdoms (a Chinese history book) as Gojamidongguk, one of the twelve states of Byeonhan. The Goseong County Office guesses that Sogaya (Gojaguk) was founded around AD 42, and says it was joined to Silla around 562. In 757 (the 16th year of King Gyeongdeok), the name of this town was changed to Goseong-gun.

In 1018, the 9th year of King Hyeonjong of Goryeo, it became Goseong-hyeon. In 1895, in the Joseon period, it belonged to Jinju-bu (Jinju Prefecture) and then was given the name Goseong-gun again. In 1906, six myeon (townships) from Jinju-gun were added to Goseong-gun, and the number of myeon rose to 23. In 1938, Goseong-myeon became Goseong-eup, which set it at 1 eup and 13 myeon, and this has continued to the present.

paras: Namhae-gun first appears in old records in 687, the 7th year of King Sinmun of Unified Silla. At that time it was called Jeonyasan-gun, with two hyeon (small districts), Nanpo-hyeon and Pyeongsan-hyeon, under it. In 757 (the 16th year of King Gyeongdeok), the name changed to Namhae-gun. In 1018, the 9th year of King Hyeonjong of Goryeo, it became Namhae-hyeon, and a hyeonnyeong (district magistrate) was placed there.

From 1592, when the Imjin War and the Jeongyu War (the Japanese invasions of Korea) broke out, Namhae was a battlefield for seven years, and at one point it became almost empty of people. In 1895, Namhae-hyeon became Namhae-gun, and in 1906, Changseondo Island was added to Namhae-gun. In 1979, Namhae-myeon became an eup. In 1986, Sangju and Mijo became myeon, so today the county has 1 eup and 9 myeon.

paras: Hadong-gun is at the far west of Gyeongsangnam-do. Jirisan Mountain is to the north, the Seomjingang River is to the west, and the South Sea is to the south. To the east it connects with Jinju-si and Sacheon-si. It was originally called Handasa-gun, and in 757 it was renamed Hadong-gun. In the Goryeo period it was called Hadong-hyeon and belonged to Jinju-mok (a large provincial district).

At the foot of Hwagae-myeon is Ssanggyesa Temple, an old temple that has been there since the Silla period, and at the foot of Banyabong Peak in Jirisan Mountain is Chilbulsa Temple. The county office also says there is the scenery of Baeksacheongsong (white sand and old pine trees together) and of Hadong Pogu Palsimni (the "eighty-ri" Hadong riverside). In 1704 it was raised to Hadong-dohobu (protectorate). In 1895 it became Hadong-gun in Jinju-bu (Jinju Prefecture). On October 1, 1938, Hadong-myeon became Hadong-eup.

paras: Polished stone tools and pottery from the Bronze Age were found in Oksan-ri, Sancheong-eup, and Deokgyo-ri, Samjang-myeon. In 757, the 16th year of King Gyeongdeok of Silla, this area became Saneum-hyeon and belonged to Gwolseong-gun. In 1767, the 43rd year of King Yeongjo of Joseon, Saneum-hyeon was renamed Sancheong-hyeon. In 1895 Sancheong-hyeon became Sancheong-gun and Danseong-hyeon became Danseong-gun.

Dansoksa Temple was built in the reign of King Gyeongdeok of Silla, and the county office history says that temples such as Dansoksa and Samjangsa were built and the area grew into a major center of Buddhism. In 1363, Mun Ik-jeom brought cotton seeds from Yuan China. In 1561, Nammyeong Jo Sik built Sancheonjae (a place of study). In 1914, Danseong-gun was merged into Sancheong-gun. In 1967, Jirisan National Park was designated, and in 1979, Sancheong-myeon became Sancheong-eup.

paras: In the Silla period, Hamyang-gun was called Sokham-gun or Hamseong, and in 757 its name was changed to Cheollyeong-gun. In 1010, in the Goryeo period, it became Hamyang-gun (含陽郡), and in 1172 it was lowered to a hyeon (small district). In Hamyang, the Yeo, O and Bak families lived as the local family clans. In 1395, in the Joseon period, it was raised to a gun, in 1629 it became a hyeon, in 1729 it was raised to Hamyang-bu, and in 1788 it became Hamyang-gun again.

On March 1, 1914, Anui-gun was abolished and some of its myeon (townships) were added to Hamyang-gun. In 1933, Daeji-myeon was merged into Anui-myeon. On October 21, 1957, Seokbok-myeon was merged into Hamyang-myeon, which was raised to Hamyang-eup.

paras: In the Gaya period, Geochang was one place in the Daegaya confederation. Since long ago it was called names such as Geoyeol, Geota and Arim, from the meaning "wide, big, bright field." The Geochang County Office says it was first called "Geochang" in 757, the 16th year of King Gyeongdeok of Silla.

In 1018, in the Goryeo period, it was a hyeon (small district) under Hapju. In 1414, in the Joseon period, it was joined with Geoje to become Jechang-hyeon, and in 1739 it was raised to Geochang-bu. In 1895, Geochang-bu became Geochang-gun, and in 1914 some land from Anui-gun and Samga-gun was added. In 1937, Geochang-myeon became an eup. In 1957, Wolcheon-myeon was added to Geochang-eup, and today the county has 1 eup and 11 myeon.

paras: Hapcheon-gun is in the mountainous inland area in the northwest of Gyeongsangnam-do. In 757, in Unified Silla, it was called Gangyang-gun, and in 1018, in the Goryeo period, it was raised to Hapju. The name Hapcheon came in 1413, the 13th year of King Taejong of Joseon, when Hapju was lowered to Hapcheon-gun. The county office explains this name as meaning "narrow stream."

In March 1914, Chogye-gun and Samga-gun were merged into Hapcheon-gun, and in May 1979, Hapcheon-myeon became an eup. In the north, the Gayasan Mountain range stretches out, and many large and small mountains branch off from it. The Hwanggang River, a branch of the Nakdonggang River, starts at Deogyusan Mountain in Geochang-gun, passes Hapcheon-eup, flows through the middle of the county, and meets the main stream of the Nakdonggang River.

paras: Jeju-si is in the middle of the northern part of Jeju Island. To the south, it meets Seogwipo-si across the top of Hallasan (Mount Halla). Its land is shaped like the northern slope of Hallasan, which gets gradually lower. It also works as the gateway to Jeju, linking air and sea travel. Islands such as Udo and Biyangdo belong to it, and both are volcanic islands.

Jeju-si is the place where, according to a story passed down, three divine men who founded Tamna (the old kingdom of Jeju) rose up from Moheunghyeol (the hole in the ground now called Samseonghyeol). The story says they welcomed three princesses who came in a wooden box, held a wedding, and then farmed and raised cattle and horses. In 1105, during the Goryeo period, Tamna-gun (Tamna County) was set up here. In 1931, it became Jeju-eup (Jeju town). On September 1, 1955, it was raised to the status of a city, Jeju-si.

paras: The timeline of Seogwipo-si says that in 1439, during the Joseon period, a fortress called Seogwijin (Seogwi Fort) was built above Hongnocheon (Hongno Stream). It says that in 1590, Seogwijin was moved to a spot above Seogwipo. In 1956, Seogwi-myeon (Seogwi township) became Seogwi-eup (Seogwi town). On July 1, 1981, Seogwi-eup and Jungmun-myeon (Jungmun township) were merged to form Seogwipo-si. On July 1, 2006, Seogwipo-si and Namjeju-gun (South Jeju County) were merged to form the Seogwipo-si of today.

Seogwipo-si is described as a place where beautiful nature stretches from Seongsan Ilchulbong (Seongsan Sunrise Peak) to Songaksan (Mount Songak), with Hallasan in the middle. It has been listed as a UNESCO World Natural Heritage site. Many tangerines are grown here, and its main work is primary industry, such as field crops, fishing, and livestock. It is also the southernmost city in Korea.

paras: Chuncheon was called Usuju in 637, under Queen Seondeok of Silla, and Suyakju in 673, under King Munmu. In 940, in the Goryeo period, it was renamed Chunju. In 1403, in the Joseon period, it was changed to its present name, Chuncheon. In 1949, Chuncheon-bu (Chuncheon Prefecture) became Chuncheon-si. In 1995, Chuncheon-si and Chuncheon-gun (Chuncheon County) were merged, and the city now has both urban and rural areas.

Chuncheon-si describes itself as a fast city, one hour from the capital area, because the Seoul-Chuncheon Expressway opened in 2009 and the Gyeongchun Line electric train opened in 2010. It has been certified as an International Slow City. It has places such as Kim Yu-jeong Literature Village and the Samaksan Ropeway (a cable car up Samaksan Mountain). The Chuncheon Mime Festival, the Chuncheon Puppet Festival, and the Dakgalbi (spicy stir-fried chicken) and Makguksu (buckwheat noodles) Festival are also held.

paras: In 678, the 18th year of King Munmu of Silla, Wonju became Bukwon Sogyeong (Bukwon Secondary Capital). Later, in the time of King Gyeongdeok, it was called Bukwongyeong (Bukwon Capital). In 940, the 23rd year of King Taejo of Goryeo, Bukwongyeong was abolished and the name Wonju was given. In 1308, the 34th year of King Chungnyeol, it became Wonju-mok (a large provincial district) and a center of administration. Wonju-si is in the southwest of Gangwon Special Self-Governing Province. Across the Namhangang River and the Seomgang River, it borders Yeoju-si in Gyeonggi-do.

In 1395, Gangneung-do (Gangneung Province) and Gyoju-do (Gyoju Province) were joined. The name Gangwon-do was made from "Gang" of Gangneung and "Won" of Wonju. At this time, Gangwon Gamyeong (the Gangwon provincial government office), the office that governed Gangwon-do, was set up in Wonju, so Wonju became the center of Gangwon-do. It became a city in 1955. On January 1, 1995, Wonju-si and Wonju-gun (Wonju County) were merged.

paras: Gangneung-si was long ago home to the Yemaek people. In the Goguryeo period it was called Haseulla. In 757, in the time of King Gyeongdeok of Silla, it became Myeongju, and in 1308, in the Goryeo period, it was changed to Gangneung-bu (Gangneung Prefecture). In 1955, Gangneung-eup, Seongdeok-myeon, and Gyeongpo-myeon were joined to form Gangneung-si. On January 1, 1995, Gangneung-si and Myeongju-gun (Myeongju County) were merged into one.

Gangneung-si is east of the Taebaek Mountains, and its eastern side is the East Sea. Pine forests and sandy beaches continue along the long coast, and the Namdaecheon Stream flows through the city. It is described as the birthplace of Saimdang and Yulgok, and of Heo Gyun and Nanseolheon. It was also a host city for ice sports (sports played on ice) at the 2018 PyeongChang Winter Olympics.

paras: Donghae-si became a city on April 1, 1980, when Mukho-eup and Bukpyeong-eup were joined. Mukho Port opened in 1941, and the next year, in 1942, Mangsang-myeon of Gangneung-gun (Gangneung County) was raised to Mukho-eup. Bukpyeong became Bukpyeong-eup of Samcheok-gun (Samcheok County) in 1945, and Bukpyeong Port opened in 1979.

The name Bukpyeong is said to come from 1631, when Yi Jun, the busa (governor) of Samcheok-bu (Samcheok Prefecture), named the area north of the Jeoncheon Stream Bukpyeong-ri. It is also said to be a Chinese-character version of Dwitdeuru, the name people used for the fields north of Samcheok-bu. In 1984, Bukpyeong Station became Donghae Station, and in 1986 the name of Bukpyeong Port was changed to Donghae Port.

paras: The name Taebaek comes from Taebaeksan Mountain. Taebaek City Hall explains that Taebaeksan means "a greatly bright mountain" and is linked to the story of Dangun. In 1981, Jangseong-eup and Hwangji-eup were merged to become a city. Both towns lie below Taebaeksan, so the city was named Taebaek-si. The representatives of the two towns first tried hard to make a Taebaek-gun (Taebaek County), but the result was a city.

In the past, the land of today's Taebaek-si was called Jangsaeng. One explanation says the name came from the many jangseung (wooden village guardian posts) set up along the road to Cheonjedan (the Heaven Altar) at the top of Taebaeksan. Names such as Jangseungbaegi and Jangseung-geori still remain. In 1994, some villages of Hajang-myeon in Samcheok-gun (Samcheok County) joined Taebaek-si, and Sajo-dong was created.

paras: Sokcho (束草) is written with the Chinese characters for "bind" and "grass." Two stories are told about the name. One says that Solsan (Pine Hill), next to Yeonggeumjeong Pavilion, looks as if pine trees and grass were tied together and set up. The other says that when the magistrate of Ulsan said he would take away Ulsanbawi Rock, the rock was tied with a rope twisted from horsetail grass growing between Cheongchoho Lake and Yeongnangho Lake, and then set on fire.

In 1937, Docheon-myeon became Sokcho-myeon, and in 1942 it became Sokcho-eup. On January 1, 1963, Sokcho-eup became Sokcho-si. In 1998, some dongs were merged, and the number of administrative dongs went from 13 to 8. At the Joyang-dong Prehistoric Site (National Historic Site No. 376), seven Bronze Age pit-house sites and two dolmens (ancient stone tombs) were found.

paras: Long ago, Samcheok-si was called Siljikguk (Siljik Kingdom). In 757, in the time of King Gyeongdeok of Silla, it became Samcheok-gun (Samcheok County). In 1393, in the Joseon period, it was raised to Samcheok-bu (Samcheok Prefecture), and in 1413 the name was changed to Samcheok Dohobu (Samcheok Protectorate). In 1895 it became Samcheok-gun again.

On January 1, 1986, Samcheok-eup became Samcheok-si. On January 1, 1995, Samcheok-si and Samcheok-gun were merged to form today's Samcheok-si. Bukpyeong-eup, which had been in Samcheok-gun, joined Donghae-si in 1980, and Jangseong-eup and Hwangji-eup were merged in 1981 to become Taebaek-si. Samcheok-si is in the southernmost part of Gangwon Special Self-Governing Province. The East Sea is to the east, Donghae-si is to the north, Jeongseon-gun and Taebaek-si are to the west, and Uljin-gun in Gyeongsangbuk-do is to the south.

paras: Hongcheon was called Beollyeokcheon-hyeon in the Goguryeo period, and in the time of King Gyeongdeok of Silla it was changed to Nokhyo. In 1018, the 9th year of King Hyeonjong of Goryeo, the name Hongcheon was given. In 1413, the 13th year of King Taejong of Joseon, it became Hongcheon-hyeon (Hongcheon County). In 1895 it became Hongcheon-hyeon of Chuncheon-bu (Chuncheon Prefecture), and in 1963 Hongcheon-myeon was raised to Hongcheon-eup.

Hongcheon County Office describes Hongcheon as a mountainous area in the center of the Korean Peninsula. The Hongcheongang River passes through the city area of Hongcheon-eup and flows west. It meets the Bukhangang River at Seorak-myeon, Gapyeong-gun, Gyeonggi-do, and there are small plains around the river. Chuncheon-si is to the north, Hoengseong-gun and Pyeongchang-gun are to the south, and to the west it borders Yangpyeong-gun in Gyeonggi-do.

paras: Hoengseong was called Hoengcheon in the Goguryeo period, and also Eosamae. In Unified Silla it was called Hwangcheon, and in Goryeo it was called Hoengcheon again. In 1389, an official called a gammu was placed there. In 1414, the 14th year of King Taejong of Joseon, it was renamed Hoengseong, and in 1895 Hoengseong-hyeon (Hoengseong County) became Hoengseong-gun.

Hoengseong-gun is in the southwest of Gangwon Special Self-Governing Province, in the middle part of Korea, in the Yeongseo region. Pyeongchang-gun is to the east, Yangpyeong-gun in Gyeonggi-do is to the west, Wonju-si and Yeongwol-gun are to the south, and Hongcheon-gun is to the north. In 1910, Seowon-myeon of Wonju-gun joined Hoengseong-gun. In 1979, Hoengseong-myeon became Hoengseong-eup, and in 1989 the area of the Gangnim Branch Office became Gangnim-myeon.

paras: Yeongwol was called Baegwol in the Baekje period, Naeseong-hyeon (Naeseong County) in the Goguryeo period, and Naeseong-gun in the Silla period. In 1167, in the Goryeo period, it became Yeongwol-hyeon (Yeongwol County), and in 1372 it became Yeongwol-gun. In 1699, in the Joseon period, it became Yeongwol Dohobu (Yeongwol Protectorate), and in 1905 Jucheon-hyeon (Jucheon County) was merged into Yeongwol-gun. In 1960, Yeongwol-myeon became Yeongwol-eup.

Yeongwol-gun is in the far south of Gangwon Special Self-Governing Province. It is an inland area with many mountains, which are part of the Taebaek, Charyeong, and Sobaek mountain ranges. Today it has 2 eup (towns) and 7 myeon (townships). Many myeon have changed their names. In 2009, Hadong-myeon became Gimsatgat-myeon and Seo-myeon became Hanbando-myeon. In 2016, Suju-myeon became Mureungdowon-myeon, and in 2021, Jungdong-myeon became Sansol-myeon.

paras: Pyeongchang is a name that began in 940, the 23rd year of King Taejo of Goryeo, when the old name Baego-hyeon (Baego County) was changed to Pyeongchang-hyeon (Pyeongchang County). It became Pyeongchang-gun in 1895. In 1906, Daehwa, Bongpyeong, and Jinbu-myeon came into Pyeongchang-gun from Gangneung. In 1979, Pyeongchang-myeon became Pyeongchang-eup, and in 1982 the county office moved to Ha-ri in Pyeongchang-eup.

In 2009, Pyeongchang-gun announced "Pyeongchang, Forest Capital." In 2011, it was confirmed as the host of the 2018 Pyeongchang Winter Olympics. The Winter Olympics were held in February 2018, and the Winter Paralympics in March. In 2007, Doam-myeon changed its name to Daegwallyeong-myeon. In 2019, the county held a ceremony to announce Pyeongchang as a city of peace and Balwangsan (Mount Balwang) as a famous mountain.

paras: Jeongseon was once the land of Yemaek. In the Three Kingdoms period it became Goguryeo land, and it was called Ingmae-hyeon (Ingmae County) at that time. In 757, in the Silla period, its name was changed to Jeongseon-hyeon (Jeongseon County). In the Goryeo period it was raised to Jeongseon-gun. It was also renamed with names such as Dowon and Simbong, but in 1353 it became Jeongseon again.

The Jeongseon County Office says the Taebaek Mountains form a watershed here that divides Yeongdong (the area east of the mountains) from Yeongseo (the area west of them). There are mountains such as Sangwonsan, Gariwangsan (Mount Gariwang), and Bibongsan. The Songcheon River meets the Imgyecheon Stream at Yeoryang-ri to form "Auraji," and then meets the Odaecheon Stream at Nampyeong-ri. Jeongseon-eup has been the home of the county office since the Joseon period, and Jeongseon-myeon became Jeongseon-eup in 1973.

paras: In the Goguryeo period, Cheorwon was called Cheorwon or Moeuldongbi, and King Gyeongdeok of Silla changed the name to Cheolseong. It is said that in 901, Gungye founded a country, and in 905 he moved his capital to Pungcheonwon in Cheorwon. In 919 the name Dongju came into use. In 1895 it became Cheorwon-gun in Chuncheon-bu (Chuncheon Prefecture), and the next year it became Cheorwon-gun in Gangwon-do (Gangwon Province).

In 1963, several eup and myeon of the former Gimhwa-gun came into Cheorwon-gun. In 1979 Galmal-myeon, and in 1980 Dongsong-myeon, were raised to eup. The Hantan River flows between Dongsong-eup and Galmal-eup and runs into the Imjin River. The middle and southwest parts are hills and plains that suit farming, and the area is said to be known as a land that produces a lot of grain.

paras: In the Goguryeo period, Hwacheon was called Saengcheon-gun or Yasimae, and in the Unified Silla period it was called Nangcheon. In 1902, the 39th year of King Gojong of Joseon, the name was changed to Hwacheon (written with the Chinese characters 華川), and it has been used ever since. Sanae-myeon came into Hwacheon-gun in 1954, and in 1979 Hwacheon-myeon became Hwacheon-eup.

Hwacheon-gun is a mountainous area with many mountains. The Gwangju Mountains stretch along the west and a branch of the Taebaek Mountains along the east, and the Bukhan River, which starts at Geumgangsan (Mount Kumgang), flows south. In 1910, Haseo-myeon and Nam-myeon were merged into Hanam-myeon, and Ganchok-myeon and Wondong-myeon were merged into Gandong-myeon. It is said that in 1941, when Hwacheon Dam was built, the Gandong-myeon office was moved from Guman-ri to Yuchon-ri.

paras: In the Goguryeo period, Yanggu was called "Yoeunhol-cha," and in 757, in the reign of King Gyeongdeok of Silla, it became Yangrok-gun. The name Yanggu (written with the Chinese characters 楊口) is said to come from 1592. A newly appointed governor was passing through the first town on the road to Geumgangsan (Mount Kumgang), saw a forest of huge weeping willows, and called the place "Yanggu." It is said the name has been used ever since.

On May 1, 1979, Yanggu-myeon became Yanggu-eup. On January 1, 2021, Nam-myeon changed its name to Gukto-jeongjungang-myeon ("the center of the country"). Measured by satellite, the point at the middle of Korea's land was confirmed to be San 48, Dochon-ri, in Gukto-jeongjungang-myeon. Yanggu-gun has Inje-gun to the east, Hwacheon-gun to the west, and Chuncheon-si (Chuncheon City) to the south. To the north, it faces North Korea across the Military Demarcation Line.

paras: Inje-gun is in the northern part of Yeongseo in Gangwon Special Self-Governing Province, centered on the Baekdudaegan (the main mountain range of Korea). The Inje County Office says that this area was Jeojok-hyeon in the Goguryeo period and was changed to Huije-hyeon in the Silla period. In 1896 Inje became a gun (county). In 1954 it took over administrative authority from the military government and got back most of its old administrative districts, and in 1979 Inje-myeon was raised to Inje-eup.

Most of the land is mountains and forest. Part of Seoraksan National Park and Soyang Lake lie in Inje-gun, and the county office describes mountains such as Jeombongsan, Bangtaesan, and Daeamsan, and streams such as Naerincheon and Inbukcheon. There are several high mountain ridges over 800 m above sea level. The Seoul-Yangyang Expressway and National Route 44, which goes to the East Sea coast, pass through the county, and it also touches the Military Demarcation Line.

paras: Long ago, Goseong-gun and Ganseong-gun were separate. In 1914 Goseong-gun was merged into Ganseong-gun. In 1919 Ganseong-gun was abolished and its name was changed to Goseong-gun, and part of Imnam-myeon in Tongcheon-gun was added too. In 1954, under the Act on Temporary Administrative Measures for Recovered Areas, it took charge of four myeon south of the Military Demarcation Line: Ganseong, Gojin, Hyeonnae, and Sudong.

In 1963, Jukwang-myeon and Toseong-myeon of Yangyang-gun came into Goseong-gun. Gojin-myeon became an eup in 1973, and Ganseong-myeon became one in 1979. Goseong-gun is in the northeast of Gangwon Special Self-Governing Province. To the north it faces Tongcheon-gun across Geumgangsan (Mount Kumgang), and to the west it touches Inje-gun across Hyangnobong (Hyangno Peak). To the east is the East Sea.

paras: The name Yangyang was given because the land and natural beauty here were said to be similar to Xiangyang, which sits on the Han River in Hubei Province, China. It has been used since 1416. In that year Yangju Dohobu (Yangju Protectorate) became Yangyang Dohobu (Yangyang Protectorate), and in 1895 the name was changed to Yangyang-gun.

In May 1919, Ganseong-gun was abolished, and Toseong-myeon and Jukwang-myeon came into Yangyang-gun. On January 1, 1963, Sokcho-eup was separated from Yangyang-gun and became a city. Jukwang-myeon and Toseong-myeon went to Goseong-gun, and Hyeonnam-myeon of Myeongju-gun became part of Yangyang-gun again. On May 1, 1979, Yangyang-myeon became Yangyang-eup, and in 1983 part of Sangbok-ri in Ganghyeon-myeon was merged into Sokcho-si (Sokcho City).

paras: The name Jeonju has been used since the time of King Gyeongdeok of Silla, in 757. Before that, in the Baekje period, it was called Wansan. The Jeonju City website explains that the letters "wan" and "jeon" both stand for the Korean word "on," which means "whole."

In 900, Gyeon Hwon made it the capital of Later Baekje. In the Joseon period, in 1403, it was named Jeonju-bu (Jeonju Prefecture), and in 1894 the Donghak Revolution army took Jeonju-bu. In 1935, Jeonju-eup was raised to Jeonju-bu and split off from Jeonju-gun, and Jeonju-gun was renamed Wanju-gun. It became Jeonju-si in 1949. In 1957, part of the land of Wanju-gun was added to Jeonju-si, and in 1989 Wansan-gu and Deokjin-gu were created.

paras: Wansan-gu started as a branch office on July 1, 1988, and became a district (gu) on May 1, 1989. At that time there was no law on resident votes yet, so a naming committee of 24 people from many fields met, talked it over, and chose the name.

Wansan was the name of the land that meant Jeonju in the Baekje period. The name is thought to come from a mountain peak called Wansan Chilbong (Wansan Seven Peaks). An old story says the peak looks like the Big Dipper (Bukdu Chilseong) that came down to earth, with Namcheon and Seocheon streams as the Milky Way. Today, Wansan-gu has 19 administrative neighborhoods (haengjeong-dong), such as Jungang-dong, Pungnam-dong, and Seosin-dong.

paras: Deokjin-gu also opened as a branch office on July 1, 1988, and became a district (gu) on May 1, 1989. Together with Wansan-gu, its name was chosen after a naming committee of 24 people from many fields talked it over.

Deokjin means "big ferry crossing." In an old book, the Dongguk Yeoji Seungnam (an old geography book of Korea), it is written as Deokjin-mot (Deokjin Pond). The name is said to come from the idea that a ferry crossing never runs dry and always flows with plenty, and from the idea that a mountain enjoys virtue only when it has water. It was chosen to pair with Wansan, so that mountain and water go together. Today, Deokjin-gu has 16 administrative neighborhoods (haengjeong-dong).

paras: Long ago, Gunsan was part of the land of Mahan (an early Korean confederation). In the Baekje period it was called by names such as Maseoryang and Bubuli-hyeon. In the 16th year of King Gyeongdeok of Unified Silla, it was given the name Okgu-hyeon. In the 6th year of King Hyeonjong of Goryeo, it came to belong to the neighboring Impi-hyeon. In 1380, the 6th year of King U of Goryeo, General Choe Mu-seon used cannons to defeat 500 Japanese pirate ships on the Geumgang River (Geum River).

In 1899, Gunsan became an open port (gaehangjang), where ships could come and go. In 1949, Gunsan-bu was renamed Gunsan-si. In 1990, the Geumgang Estuary Barrage (Geumgang Hagutdeuk) was built and joined Jeonbuk and South Chungcheong. On January 1, 1995, Gunsan-si and Okgu-gun were joined, and Gunsan became the present city, which has both city and countryside.

paras: Iksan is said to have had a state called Geonmaguk, one of the 54 states of Mahan (an early Korean confederation). King Onjo of Baekje joined Mahan and called this place Geummajeo. In 1914, Hamyeol-hyeon, Yongan-hyeon, and Yeosan-gun were joined to form Iksan-gun, and that same year Namil-myeon and Dongil-myeon were joined to form Iksan-myeon.

In 1931, Iksan-myeon was raised to Iksan-eup and then renamed Iri-eup. In 1947, Iri-eup became Iri-bu and was separated from Iksan-gun. It became Iri-si in 1949, and in 1979 the Iksan-gun office moved from Iri-si to Hamyeol-eup. On May 10, 1995, Iri-si and Iksan-gun were joined to become the present Iksan-si.

paras: The name Jeongeup began to be used in 757, when King Gyeongdeok of Silla changed the name of Jeongchon-hyeon, a Baekje town, to Jeongeup-hyeon. In 1894, the harsh rule of Jo Byeong-gap, the governor of Gobu-gun, led to the Gobu Peasant Uprising, which spread into the Gabo Donghak Peasant Revolution. In 1895, Jeongeup-hyeon became Jeongeup-gun, and in 1914 Jeongeup, Gobu, and Taein were joined to form Jeongeup-gun.

In 1589, Yi Sun-sin came to Jeongeup as the magistrate (hyeongam). Jeongeup-myeon became Jeongju-eup in 1931 and Jeongju-si in 1981. In 1995, the city and the county were joined, and the name became Jeongeup-si. In the southeast are Naejangsan National Park and Ipamsan (Mt. Ipam), and in the northwest the wide Dongjin Plain spreads out.

paras: In 1895, Namwon-bu became Namwon-gun, and in 1906 some of its townships (myeon) were passed to Imsil-gun, Jangsu-gun, and Gurye-gun. In 1981, Namwon-eup was raised to a city, and the area was split into Namwon-gun and Namwon-si. On January 1, 1995, Namwon-si and Namwon-gun were joined into one, and Namwon became a city with both city and countryside.

Namwon City Hall guesses that people began to live here in the Bronze Age or later. Bronze Age remains include dolmens (jiseokmyo, stone tombs), and in 1991 rock carvings thought to be from the Bronze Age were found. It is said that many relics linked to Gaya (an ancient Korean confederation) were found in tombs in Inwol-myeon and Ayeong-myeon in the Unbong area.

paras: Gimje is said to have been a state called Byeokbiriguk in the Samhan period (the Three Han states). In the 27th year of King Biryu of Baekje it was given the name Byeokgol-gun, and in the 16th year of King Gyeongdeok of Unified Silla its name changed to Gimje-gun. In the 21st year of King Injong of Goryeo it became Gimje-hyeon, and in 1466 it became Gimje-gun again. On January 1, 1995, Gimje-si and Gimje-gun were joined into one.

In Buryang-myeon, Gimje, there is Byeokgolje (Byeokgol Reservoir), which is introduced as the largest ancient reservoir in Korea. The Samguk Sagi (History of the Three Kingdoms) says that Byeokgolji was first opened in AD 330, and in 1963 it became National Historic Site No. 111. "Manggyeong" in Manggyeong-eup, Gimje, means "ten thousand rice-paddy ridges" when read letter by letter, which is said to mean that the fields are wide.

paras: Wanju-gun is in the center of Jeonbuk Special Self-Governing Province, and it surrounds Jeonju-si all the way around. On the east it touches Jinan-gun, on the west Gimje-si, on the south Imsil-gun and Jeongeup-si, and on the north Iksan-si and, in South Chungcheong Province, Nonsan-si and Geumsan-gun. In the Samhan period it was land of Mahan. In 1914, Gosan-gun was joined to it to form Jeonju-gun, and in 1935, when Jeonju-eup was raised to Jeonju-bu, the county was renamed Wanju-gun.

Wanju-gun is a place with many mountains. It has Godeoksan (Mt. Godeok) and Moaksan (Mt. Moak), and the Jeonbuk Plain spreads out to the northwest. Soyangcheon, Gosancheon, and Samcheoncheon streams all flow into the Mangyeonggang River (Mangyeong River). The Jeolla Line railway runs through it from north to south. In 2012, the county office moved to Jiam-ro in Yongjin-eup, and in 2015 Yongjin-myeon became Yongjin-eup.

paras: In the Baekje period, Jinan-gun was called Nanjinah-hyeon, and in 757, in the Unified Silla period, its name changed to Jinan. In 1413, Maryeong-hyeon was joined to it to form Jinan-hyeon, and in 1895 it became Jinan-gun. In 1914 it was joined with Yongdam-gun to become today's Jinan-gun, and in 1979 Jinan-myeon became an eup.

Jinan-gun is in the mountainous east of Jeonbuk Special Self-Governing Province. On the east it touches Muju-gun, on the south Jangsu-gun and Imsil-gun, on the west Wanju-gun, and on the north Geumsan-gun in South Chungcheong Province. The Jinan Plateau, formed by the Sobaek Mountains and the Noryeong Mountains, is here. Jinan Yongdam Dam, which was started in 1992 and finished in 2001, sends drinking water and household water to Jeonbuk and the Chungcheong region.

paras: The name Muju was made from the first letters of two old towns, Mupung and Jugye. In the Three Kingdoms period, Mupung, which was Silla land, was called Musan-hyeon, and Jugye, which was Baekje land, was called Jeokcheon-hyeon. In 1414, the 14th year of King Taejong of Joseon, the two were joined into one, and the name Muju was born. In 1895 it became Muju-gun, and in 1914 Bunam-myeon of Geumsan came into Muju.

Muju-gun is on the Sobaek Mountains, so it touches both South and North Chungcheong Provinces and both South and North Gyeongsang Provinces. It is introduced as a place that is beautiful in all four seasons, with Deogyusan (Mt. Deogyu) National Park at its center. It is also said that, because of the expressways, you can reach Muju from anywhere in the country, such as Seoul or Busan, in about two hours.

paras: Jangsu-gun is in the east of Jeonbuk Special Self-Governing Province. On the south it touches Namwon-si, on the west Imsil-gun and Jinan-gun, and on the north Muju-gun. The Samguk Sagi (History of the Three Kingdoms) says that in the Baekje period this area had Baekhae-gun and Upyeong-hyeon. Baekhae-gun was on the side of today's Janggye-myeon, and Upyeong-hyeon on the side of Jangsu-eup. In 1018 they were renamed Janggye-hyeon and Jangsu-hyeon.

In 1895, Jangsu-hyeon became Jangsu-gun, and in 1906 Sanseo-myeon and Beonam-myeon of Namwon-gun were added, giving it a shape close to today's. In 1979, Jangsu-myeon became Jangsu-eup, and in 1993 Gyenae-myeon was renamed Janggye-myeon. Many Gaya sites (Gaya was an ancient Korean confederation) have been confirmed in Jangsu-gun, and in 2019 the Dongchon-ri Tumuli Group (Dongchon-ri Gobungun) became the first national historic site in Jangsu-gun.

paras: Imsil-gun belonged to Mahan (an early Korean confederation) in the Samhan period, and in the Baekje period it was called Inghil-gun. In 759, in the Unified Silla period, Inghil-gun was renamed Imsil-gun. In 1413 it became Imsil-hyeon, in 1895 it was changed to Imsil-gun, and in 1906 six districts (bang) of Namwon-bu came into Imsil-gun.

The county's timeline lists the Stone Lantern at the Imsil Jingusa Temple Site (8th to 9th century) as Treasure No. 267. It also says that the tale of the loyal dog of Osu (Osu Uigyeon) appears in the Bohanjip, written by Choe Ja in 1250. In 1920, the Imsil-gun office was built on the site of the old government office, and in 2010 it moved to a new building at 30 Sujeong-ro. In 1979, Imsil-myeon became an eup.

paras: Sunchang-gun had a different name in each period. In the Mahan period it was called Osan and Okcheon, in the Baekje period Dosil, and in the Unified Silla period Sunhwa. In the Goryeo period it became Sunchang-hyeon and belonged to Namwon-bu. In 1314, the 1st year of King Chungsuk, it became Sunchang-gun, and in 1979 Sunchang-myeon was raised to Sunchang-eup.

Sunchang-gun is in the south-center of Jeonbuk Special Self-Governing Province. The Honam Jeongmaek (Honam Mountain Ridge) runs through it, so it is mountain country and most of the land is mountains. On the east, across the Seomjingang River (Seomjin River), it touches Namwon-si, on the west Jeongeup-si, and on the north Imsil-gun. On the south it touches parts of Jangseong-gun, Damyang-gun, and Gokseong-gun in South Jeolla. Rivers such as the Seomjingang River and the Jeokseonggang River flow in the south and east.

paras: Gochang-gun is at the southwest end of Jeonbuk Special Self-Governing Province. On the northeast it touches Jeongeup-si and Buan-gun, on the southeast Jangseong-gun and Yeonggwang-gun in South Jeolla, and on the northwest there is the West Sea (Yellow Sea). Today's Gochang-gun was formed in 1914 when the three towns of Gochang, Mujang, and Heungdeok were joined into one. In 1955, Gochang-myeon was raised to Gochang-eup.

Before they were joined, Gochang was originally Moryangbuli-hyeon of Baekje, and in the 16th year of King Gyeongdeok of Silla its name changed to Gochang-hyeon. Mujang was formed when two towns, Musong and Jangsa, were joined, and in the 17th year of King Taejong of Joseon it was given the name Mujang. Heungdeok changed from Jangdeok to Changdeok to Heungdeok in the Goryeo period. It is said that the name was changed to avoid using a king's name.

paras: The name Buan was set in 1416. One letter each was taken from Buryeong-hyeon ("bu") and Boan-hyeon ("an"), and the place was called Buan-hyeon. In 1895, when the names of bu, mok, gun, and hyeon across the country were all changed to gun, it became Buan-gun.

In the Baekje period, Buan was an important place for politics, the military, and the sea, and it was divided into two districts, Gaehwa and Heullyangmae. At Jukmak-dong there is a site where people held rites for the sea. Juryuseong is said to have been the starting point and the capital of the effort to bring Baekje back after it fell. Wido (Wi Island) went to Yeonggwang-gun in South Jeolla in 1914 and came back to Buan-gun in 1963. In 1978, the Gyehwado land reclamation work was finished, and the land grew larger.
